purpose: A language-independent inventory of capability atoms that a system claiming to represent mathematical reasoning may be scored against. It is specified without reference to any particular implementation: the question behind every atom is 'what would a faithful representation of mathematics have to be able to express?', not 'what does some existing system happen to provide?'.

scope.in_scope: Mathematical and scientific reasoning: logic and foundations, number systems, algebra, analysis, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, geometry and topology, optimisation, units and dimensions, numerical method semantics, epistemic status of statements, and meaning-preserving transformation.
scope.out_of_scope: General-purpose software concerns are excluded by construction: networking, HTTP, user interfaces, filesystems, persistence, concurrency primitives, business-domain objects, serialisation formats. A system is neither credited nor penalised for them.

criticality_definition.CRITICAL: A representation lacking this atom cannot faithfully express a broad and important class of mathematics at all; the gap is not closable by user-level composition.
criticality_definition.HIGH: Absence blocks or distorts a substantial, frequently occurring class of statements, or forces an encoding that loses semantics.
criticality_definition.MEDIUM: Absence is a real limitation within one domain but is usually workaroundable with an explicit, faithful encoding.
criticality_definition.LOW: Specialised or boundary-marking. Included to delimit the space and to probe hidden assumptions, not as an expectation.

size_note: The design target for V1 was 300-450 atoms. The delivered ontology exceeds the upper end of that range. No atom was removed to hit the number: every atom present names a capability that some class of mathematical statement genuinely requires, and cutting to a quota would have made coverage a function of an arbitrary budget rather than of the subject matter. Scoring is weight-based, so the extra LOW-weight atoms shift aggregate scores only slightly; they exist mainly to delimit the space and to probe hidden assumptions.

atoms.name: alpha-equivalence
atoms.essential_semantics: Renaming bound variables does not change identity; two alpha-equivalent statements must canonicalise to the same form.
atoms.canonical_example: forall x. P(x) equals forall y. P(y)
atoms.rationale: Without alpha-equivalence, structural comparison of statements is meaningless and deduplication/caching is unsound.

atoms.name: function application
atoms.essential_semantics: Applies a function to arguments with arity and domain checking; distinguishable from multiplication by juxtaposition.
atoms.canonical_example: f(x + 1) versus f * (x + 1)
atoms.rationale: Ambiguity between application and multiplication is a classic notational failure; the representation must disambiguate it structurally.

atoms.name: axiom / postulate declaration
atoms.essential_semantics: A proposition accepted without proof, explicitly marked as such and attributable to a theory.
atoms.canonical_example: Axiom of Choice
atoms.rationale: Distinguishing what is assumed from what is derived is the minimal epistemic hygiene of a formal system.

atoms.name: biconditional / iff
atoms.essential_semantics: Symmetric entailment between propositions, distinct from equality of terms and from definitional equality.
atoms.canonical_example: n is even iff n mod 2 = 0
atoms.rationale: Characterisation theorems are biconditionals; representing them as equalities of terms is a type error.

atoms.name: relativised (bounded) quantification
atoms.essential_semantics: Quantification restricted by a guard, with the standard asymmetry: bounded-forall unfolds to implication, bounded-exists to conjunction.
atoms.canonical_example: for all x in R with x > 0, log(x) is defined
atoms.rationale: Guarded quantification is how side conditions attach to theorems; mis-unfolding it (using conjunction under forall) silently changes the claim.

atoms.name: cartesian product and tuples
atoms.essential_semantics: Product of sets/types with projection; n-ary tuples with positional typing.
atoms.canonical_example: R^2 = R x R; (x, y) with x, y : R
atoms.rationale: Joint distributions, relations, and multivariate domains all require products; encoding them as untyped lists loses arity and component types.

atoms.name: choice / selection of witnesses
atoms.essential_semantics: Selecting an element from each member of a family, with the use of choice recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: choosing a representative from each equivalence class
atoms.rationale: Included because Skolemisation and 'let x be such that' silently invoke it; a system should at least be able to name the assumption.

atoms.name: excluded middle / constructivity marker
atoms.essential_semantics: Whether a statement or proof relies on excluded middle, double-negation elimination or choice is recorded rather than assumed.
atoms.canonical_example: a non-constructive existence proof by contradiction is flagged as such
atoms.rationale: Matters only for systems that intend to extract computation from proofs, but silently assuming classical logic is a real semantic commitment.

atoms.name: conjunction
atoms.essential_semantics: Binary connective on propositions, associative in meaning, with explicit precedence relative to disjunction and implication.
atoms.canonical_example: x > 0 and x < 1
atoms.rationale: Half of all mathematical hypotheses are conjunctions of side conditions; without it, constraints cannot be bundled.

atoms.name: conservativity of definitional extension
atoms.essential_semantics: Adding a definition must not permit new theorems in the original vocabulary; definitional well-formedness conditions (fresh name, no free variables, termination for recursion) are checked.
atoms.canonical_example: defining choose(n,k) := n!/(k!(n-k)!) proves nothing new about factorials
atoms.rationale: Established metatheoretic criterion; it is what makes a standard library safe to grow, and it is mechanically checkable.

atoms.name: definition versus assertion
atoms.essential_semantics: Introducing a new name with a defining body is a distinct speech act from asserting that two existing terms are equal; definitions are conservative and non-recursive unless declared.
atoms.canonical_example: define f(x) := x^2 + 1, versus assert f(2) = 5
atoms.rationale: If definitions and assertions are the same construct, a system cannot tell a stipulation from a claim needing proof.

atoms.name: types depending on values
atoms.essential_semantics: A type may mention a term (vector of length n, n x m matrix, simplex of dimension k) and typing must respect the dependency.
atoms.canonical_example: A : Matrix(m, n), x : Vector(n), Ax : Vector(m)
atoms.rationale: Shape correctness in linear algebra is a dependent-typing problem; without it, conformability is unchecked and errors surface only at runtime.

atoms.name: sum / disjoint union type
atoms.essential_semantics: A tagged alternative between cases, with injections and case analysis; distinguishable from ordinary set union.
atoms.canonical_example: an extended value is either a real or the symbol undefined
atoms.rationale: Piecewise and partial constructions need tagged alternatives; untagged unions lose which branch was taken.

atoms.name: disjunction
atoms.essential_semantics: Inclusive binary connective; must be distinguishable from exclusive disjunction and from case-splitting control flow.
atoms.canonical_example: x = 0 or x = 1
atoms.rationale: Disjunctive conclusions (root of a quadratic, case splits) are pervasive and are not expressible by conjunction alone.

atoms.name: equality as an assertion
atoms.essential_semantics: A symmetric relation between two terms of compatible type, asserting identity; must be distinguished from assignment, from definition, from approximation, and from 'distributed as'.
atoms.canonical_example: e^{i pi} = -1
atoms.rationale: The overloading of '=' across assertion, definition, assignment and approximation is the classic source of semantic collapse in mathematical notation.

atoms.name: exclusive disjunction
atoms.essential_semantics: Connective true exactly when operands differ; must be distinguishable from inclusive or.
atoms.canonical_example: exactly one of x < 0, x > 0 holds when x != 0
atoms.rationale: Derivable but frequently needed; its absence forces verbose encodings and invites mis-reading of 'or'.

atoms.name: existential quantification
atoms.essential_semantics: Binds a variable over a domain and asserts the body for at least one element; must not be silently Skolemised into a named constant unless that transformation is recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: there exists x in R with x^2 = 2
atoms.rationale: Existence claims are the other half of mathematics; their interaction with universals is where representational systems most often fail.

atoms.name: unique existence
atoms.essential_semantics: Asserts existence together with uniqueness up to the ambient equality; must be distinguishable from plain existence.
atoms.canonical_example: there is exactly one identity element in a group
atoms.rationale: Uniqueness licenses definite description ('the' inverse, 'the' minimiser); losing it makes definitions unjustified.

atoms.name: universal quantification
atoms.essential_semantics: Binds a variable over an explicitly given domain and asserts the body for every element; the binder, the domain, and the body must be separately recoverable from the representation.
atoms.canonical_example: for all x in R, x^2 >= 0
atoms.rationale: Nearly every mathematical theorem is universally quantified; a language that cannot bind a variable over a domain cannot state theorems at all.

atoms.name: free versus bound occurrence distinction
atoms.essential_semantics: Free variables of an expression are computable and distinguished from bound ones; a statement with unintended free variables must be rejected or flagged.
atoms.canonical_example: x^2 + y has free {x, y}; forall x. x^2 + y has free {y}
atoms.rationale: Closedness is the criterion for a well-posed statement; systems that ignore it accept open formulas as if they were theorems.

atoms.name: functional completeness of the connective set
atoms.essential_semantics: The available connectives must generate every Boolean function of their arguments (e.g. {not, and} or {not, or} or NAND alone).
atoms.canonical_example: any truth table on 3 propositional variables is expressible
atoms.rationale: A classical established criterion (Post 1941); it is the correct formal notion of 'complete' at the propositional layer and is mechanically checkable.

atoms.name: function as a first-class object
atoms.essential_semantics: A function may be named, passed, returned, quantified over, and its domain/codomain inspected, without being applied.
atoms.canonical_example: the operator D maps f to f'
atoms.rationale: Operators, transforms, estimators and objectives all take functions as arguments; a language where functions only exist to be called cannot express them.

atoms.name: typed context of assumptions
atoms.essential_semantics: An ordered context of variable declarations and assumptions under which a judgement holds; entering and leaving a context is explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: Gamma = {n : Nat, n > 3} entails n^2 > 9
atoms.rationale: Local assumptions inside a proof or a function body are contexts; a global-only assumption store cannot represent them without leaking.

atoms.name: material implication
atoms.essential_semantics: Directed connective between propositions whose semantics is truth-functional entailment, explicitly NOT correlation, causation, or a rewrite rule.
atoms.canonical_example: if n is even then n^2 is even
atoms.rationale: Implication is the backbone of theorem statements; conflating it with causation or with statistical association is a first-order semantic error.

atoms.name: indexed family of objects
atoms.essential_semantics: A map from an index set to objects, where the index is a bound variable and the family is itself an object; the index set must be explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: (X_i)_{i in I} a family of random variables
atoms.rationale: Sequences, families of random variables, matrices-as-families and parameter vectors all need indexing as a semantic construct, not as an array subscript.

atoms.name: indexed and countable set operations
atoms.essential_semantics: Union/intersection over an index set, including countably infinite index sets.
atoms.canonical_example: intersection over n in N of (0, 1/n) = empty set
atoms.rationale: Countable operations are the defining closure property of sigma-algebras and measures; finite-only set algebra cannot express measure theory.

atoms.name: induction principle over an inductive domain
atoms.essential_semantics: Base case plus step case licensing a universally quantified conclusion, over naturals or a general well-founded order.
atoms.canonical_example: sum_{i=1..n} i = n(n+1)/2 for all n in N
atoms.rationale: Induction is the only general route to universally quantified facts about infinite discrete domains.

atoms.name: anonymous function abstraction
atoms.essential_semantics: Forms a function from a bound variable and a body, with the variable's domain recoverable.
atoms.canonical_example: x |-> x^2 on R
atoms.rationale: Integrands, objectives and transforms are anonymous functions; forcing every function to be named distorts the structure of the statement.

atoms.name: modal qualification (necessity, possibility)
atoms.essential_semantics: A statement may be qualified as necessary, possible, or holding in a specified regime, with the modality not collapsing into truth.
atoms.canonical_example: it is possible that the sequence diverges
atoms.rationale: Rarely needed in core mathematics, but modelling assumptions and applicability regimes are naturally modal and are otherwise lost to prose.

atoms.name: satisfaction relation (model models formula)
atoms.essential_semantics: The relation between a structure and a sentence it makes true, distinguishing syntactic derivability from semantic truth.
atoms.canonical_example: (Z, +) satisfies the group axioms
atoms.rationale: Needed to state independence and consistency results; optional for applied mathematics but foundational for a formal system.

atoms.name: negation
atoms.essential_semantics: A unary connective on propositions with the standard truth condition; must scope explicitly over the whole proposition it negates.
atoms.canonical_example: not (x in S)
atoms.rationale: Negation is a minimal requirement for any logical fragment and interacts with quantifier scope, the most common source of representational error.

atoms.name: quantifier alternation and order sensitivity
atoms.essential_semantics: The representation must distinguish forall-x exists-y P(x,y) from exists-y forall-x P(x,y), and preserve that order through canonicalisation and round-trip.
atoms.canonical_example: pointwise convergence (forall eps exists N) vs uniform convergence (exists N forall eps)
atoms.rationale: The forall-exists / exists-forall distinction is the single most semantically load-bearing structure in analysis; a system that flattens it is not a mathematical representation.

atoms.name: partiality and definedness conditions
atoms.essential_semantics: Terms may be undefined outside a domain; the representation records the definedness precondition rather than silently producing a value.
atoms.canonical_example: 1/x is defined only for x != 0
atoms.rationale: Division, logarithm, square root and matrix inverse are partial; a total-only semantics either lies or throws away the side condition.

atoms.name: power set
atoms.essential_semantics: The set of all subsets as an object that can itself be quantified over.
atoms.canonical_example: a sigma-algebra F is a subset of P(Omega)
atoms.rationale: Topologies, sigma-algebras and hypothesis spaces are subsets of a power set; without it their type cannot be stated.

atoms.name: predicate / propositional function
atoms.essential_semantics: A named object taking terms to propositions, with declared arity and argument sorts; applying it yields a proposition, not a value.
atoms.canonical_example: Prime(n) for n : Nat
atoms.rationale: Predicate abstraction is what lifts propositional logic to mathematics; nothing about sets, quantifiers or definitions works without it.

atoms.name: proof as an inspectable object
atoms.essential_semantics: A derivation is representable, with steps, justifications and dependencies, and is checkable independently of its construction.
atoms.canonical_example: a proof of irrationality of sqrt(2) recorded as a sequence of justified steps
atoms.rationale: Only fully formal systems require this; but without any notion of derivation a system cannot claim to reason, only to state.

atoms.name: generated proof obligation / side condition
atoms.essential_semantics: The system emits the conditions that must hold for a construction to be legitimate (nonzero divisor, invertibility, convergence) as first-class items.
atoms.canonical_example: using A^{-1} generates the obligation det(A) != 0
atoms.rationale: Surfacing side conditions instead of discarding them is precisely what separates a reasoning representation from a calculator.

atoms.name: proposition as a first-class object
atoms.essential_semantics: A syntactic object denoting a truth-apt claim, distinguishable from a term/value; must be storable, nameable and referenced without being evaluated to a value.
atoms.canonical_example: P := 'every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two primes'
atoms.rationale: If claims cannot be represented separately from values, mathematics collapses into calculation and nothing can be stated, only computed.

atoms.name: quotient by an equivalence relation
atoms.essential_semantics: Construction of equivalence classes as objects, with well-definedness obligations on functions defined on the quotient.
atoms.canonical_example: Z/nZ as residue classes; functions on it must respect congruence
atoms.rationale: Modular arithmetic, projective spaces and function spaces modulo a.e. equality are quotients; ignoring well-definedness produces false statements.

atoms.name: recursive / inductive definition
atoms.essential_semantics: Definition by cases referring to smaller arguments, with an explicit termination or well-foundedness justification.
atoms.rationale: Recurrences, dynamic programming and inductive data all need it; unchecked recursion makes definitions unsound.

atoms.name: n-ary relation as an object
atoms.essential_semantics: A relation may be named, quantified over, and characterised by properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, well-founded).
atoms.canonical_example: R subset of A x A is an equivalence relation
atoms.rationale: Equivalence relations, orders and graphs are all relations; treating relations only as Boolean-valued functions loses the ability to state properties about them.

atoms.name: axiom or theorem schema with metavariables
atoms.essential_semantics: A parameterised statement standing for infinitely many instances, with metavariables distinguished from object variables.
atoms.canonical_example: the separation schema, one axiom per formula phi
atoms.rationale: Rewrite rules and generic lemmas are schemata; conflating metavariables with object variables makes instantiation unsound.

atoms.name: quantification over functions, sets or predicates
atoms.essential_semantics: A bound variable may range over functions, subsets, or predicates rather than only over individuals.
atoms.canonical_example: for every continuous f : [0,1] -> R there exists c with f(c) = integral of f
atoms.rationale: Analysis, topology and statistics quantify over functions constantly; first-order-only systems must encode this indirectly and usually lossily.

atoms.name: set-builder / separation
atoms.essential_semantics: Forms a set from a domain and a predicate, binding the comprehension variable; the domain restriction must be explicit (separation, not naive comprehension).
atoms.canonical_example: { x in R : x^2 < 2 }
atoms.rationale: Solution sets, feasible sets and events are all comprehensions; unrestricted comprehension is inconsistent, so the domain must be part of the form.

atoms.name: set membership
atoms.essential_semantics: A primitive proposition relating an element to a collection, distinct from type ascription and from subset.
atoms.canonical_example: sqrt(2) in R \ Q
atoms.rationale: Domains of quantification and function domains are stated with membership; without it the guard on a bounded quantifier cannot be written.

atoms.name: union, intersection, difference, complement
atoms.essential_semantics: Boolean algebra of sets, including complement relative to an explicitly given ambient set.
atoms.canonical_example: A union (B intersect C^c)
atoms.rationale: Event algebra in probability is exactly this; unqualified complement without an ambient set is ill-defined.

atoms.name: subset and set equality
atoms.essential_semantics: Inclusion relation between sets with extensionality; proper versus non-proper inclusion distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: Q is a proper subset of R
atoms.rationale: Structural comparison of domains, sigma-algebras and feasible regions all rest on inclusion.

atoms.name: capture-avoiding substitution
atoms.essential_semantics: Replacing a free variable by a term must not capture that term's free variables under a binder.
atoms.canonical_example: substituting y for x in exists y. x != y must rename the bound y
atoms.rationale: Substitution is the engine of instantiation and rewriting; a non-capture-avoiding implementation produces false theorems.

atoms.name: refinement types and controlled subtyping
atoms.essential_semantics: Types carrying a predicate (positive reals, unit interval, symmetric matrices), with a declared, non-arbitrary subtyping relation and explicit incomparability where appropriate.
atoms.canonical_example: sigma : {r : Real | r > 0}
atoms.rationale: Most mathematical side conditions are refinements; encoding them only as runtime assertions removes them from the statement's meaning.

atoms.name: theorem with hypotheses and conclusion
atoms.essential_semantics: A named statement with an explicit hypothesis list and a conclusion, where hypotheses are separately addressable.
atoms.canonical_example: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there is c with f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)
atoms.rationale: Theorem structure (hypotheses vs conclusion) is what allows a system to check applicability before applying a result.

atoms.name: theory / signature with axioms
atoms.essential_semantics: A bundle of sorts, operation symbols and axioms that can be instantiated by a model; models and interpretations are distinguishable from the theory.
atoms.canonical_example: the theory of groups: (G, *, e, inv) with associativity, identity, inverse axioms
atoms.rationale: Abstract algebra is organised by signatures and models; without them each structure must be re-axiomatised ad hoc.

atoms.name: truth value distinct from numeric value
atoms.essential_semantics: A Boolean-valued (or truth-value-valued) type that is not identified with 0/1 numerals and cannot be silently coerced into arithmetic.
atoms.canonical_example: (2 < 3) : Bool, and (2 < 3) + 1 is ill-typed
atoms.rationale: Conflating truth with 1/0 destroys the propositional/numeric boundary and lets nonsense such as P + 2 typecheck.

atoms.name: typing judgement
atoms.essential_semantics: An explicit judgement that a term inhabits a type/sort, checkable and reportable, distinct from set membership as a proposition.
atoms.canonical_example: x : Real
atoms.rationale: Typing is the mechanism by which nonsense is rejected; rejection of ill-formed mathematics is the core value of a mathematical IR.

atoms.name: universes / stratification of collections
atoms.essential_semantics: A discipline distinguishing sets from proper classes or a hierarchy of universes, preventing paradoxical self-membership.
atoms.canonical_example: the collection of all groups is not a set
atoms.rationale: Rarely needed for applied mathematics, but its absence is the difference between a system that can be made consistent and one that cannot be.

atoms.name: binding structure and scope
atoms.essential_semantics: The representation records which occurrences of a name are bound by which binder and where the scope ends; shadowing must be resolvable.
atoms.canonical_example: in sum over i of (sum over i of a_ij) the inner i shadows the outer
atoms.rationale: Every quantifier, integral, sum, lambda and comprehension is a binder; without a binding discipline, capture bugs make the representation unsound.

atoms.name: well-foundedness / termination measure
atoms.essential_semantics: A relation with no infinite descending chains, usable to justify recursion and induction.
atoms.canonical_example: < on N is well-founded
atoms.rationale: It is the shared precondition of induction and recursion; stating it separately makes both checkable.

atoms.name: absolute value and modulus
atoms.essential_semantics: A map to non-negative reals, defined uniformly for R and C, with the triangle inequality as a stated property.
atoms.canonical_example: |x - y| < epsilon
atoms.rationale: The epsilon-delta idiom is written with absolute value; it is the base case of norms and metrics.

atoms.name: algebraic numbers and radicals
atoms.essential_semantics: Numbers presented as roots of polynomials, with branch selection made explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: the positive root of x^2 - 2 = 0
atoms.rationale: Exact symbolic answers need it, and unstated branch choice for radicals is a genuine ambiguity.

atoms.name: cardinality, finiteness and countability
atoms.essential_semantics: Size of a set as a cardinal, with finite / countably infinite / uncountable distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: |Q| = aleph_0 < |R|
atoms.rationale: Discrete versus continuous distributions, countable additivity, and summation versus integration all hinge on cardinality.

atoms.name: complex numbers
atoms.essential_semantics: Algebraically closed field with conjugation, modulus and argument; ordering must be absent (no < on C).
atoms.canonical_example: e^{i theta} = cos theta + i sin theta
atoms.rationale: Eigenvalues, Fourier analysis and quantum formalism need C; permitting < on complex numbers is a detectable soundness failure.

atoms.name: divisibility relation
atoms.essential_semantics: The proposition d divides n, not the division operation.
atoms.rationale: Elementary number theory is stated with divisibility; expressing it only as n % d == 0 conflates a relation with a computation.

atoms.name: exact versus approximate value distinction
atoms.essential_semantics: The representation records whether a numeral denotes an exact quantity or an approximation, and does not silently promote one to the other.
atoms.canonical_example: pi versus 3.14159 (approx)
atoms.rationale: Losing exactness silently is the most common way numerical systems produce authoritative-looking wrong statements.

atoms.name: extended reals with +/- infinity
atoms.essential_semantics: R together with two infinities, with the indeterminate forms left undefined rather than given arbitrary values.
atoms.canonical_example: sup of an unbounded set is +infinity; infinity - infinity is undefined
atoms.rationale: Measure theory and optimisation routinely take values in the extended reals; treating infinity as a float sentinel destroys the distinction.

atoms.name: floor, ceiling and rounding
atoms.essential_semantics: Maps from R to Z with the tie-breaking convention explicit for rounding.
atoms.rationale: Discretisation steps depend on these, and unspecified tie-breaking is a genuine reproducibility hazard.

atoms.name: gcd and lcm
atoms.essential_semantics: Greatest common divisor / least common multiple defined by their universal properties over the divisibility order, not merely by an algorithm.
atoms.rationale: Included because it distinguishes definition-by-property from definition-by-procedure.

atoms.name: integers
atoms.essential_semantics: Ring of signed whole numbers with exact arithmetic and no rounding; distinct from a fixed-width machine integer.
atoms.canonical_example: -17 in Z
atoms.rationale: Exactness is semantic: an integer that silently wraps at 2^64 is a different mathematical object.

atoms.name: integers modulo n
atoms.essential_semantics: Quotient ring Z/nZ with residue classes as objects and congruence as the equality.
atoms.rationale: Number theory and cryptography require it, and it is the simplest quotient structure that stresses the quotient machinery.

atoms.name: intervals as domains
atoms.essential_semantics: Open, closed and half-open intervals with endpoint inclusion recorded, usable as quantification and integration domains.
atoms.canonical_example: f continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b)
atoms.rationale: The open/closed endpoint distinction is load-bearing in analysis theorems and is routinely lost when intervals are stored as bare pairs.

atoms.name: unambiguous numeric literal syntax
atoms.essential_semantics: Literals are parsed with a determinate type and value, including scientific notation, and no locale-dependent reading.
atoms.canonical_example: 1e-3 is the real 0.001, not a name
atoms.rationale: Surface-level but non-negotiable: literal ambiguity makes every downstream semantic claim unverifiable.

atoms.name: congruence and modular relations
atoms.essential_semantics: The relation a is congruent to b mod n as a proposition, distinct from the mod operator returning a residue.
atoms.canonical_example: a === b (mod n)
atoms.rationale: Congruence as a relation and mod as a function are different objects; many systems only provide the latter.

atoms.name: natural numbers
atoms.essential_semantics: An inductive type of counting numbers with a declared convention on whether 0 is included, closed under + and *, not under subtraction.
atoms.canonical_example: n in N, n >= 1
atoms.rationale: Indices, cardinalities and induction all live on N; conflating it with the integers loses the induction principle and the non-negativity guarantee.

atoms.name: non-negative reals
atoms.essential_semantics: Refinement of R by x >= 0, closed under addition and multiplication but not subtraction.
atoms.canonical_example: a variance sigma^2 >= 0
atoms.rationale: Measures, norms, variances and distances are non-negative by construction; carrying that in the type prevents whole classes of nonsense.

atoms.name: declared coercion / promotion policy
atoms.essential_semantics: Which numeric embeddings are automatic (N into Z into Q into R into C) and which require an explicit, possibly lossy, cast is specified and enforced.
atoms.canonical_example: Real to Integer requires explicit rounding; Integer to Real is automatic
atoms.rationale: Undeclared coercion is how type systems leak; the policy is a semantic commitment and must be inspectable.

atoms.name: total order on numeric domains
atoms.essential_semantics: Strict and non-strict comparison with the correct availability per domain (present on R, absent on C), and chained comparisons unambiguously parsed.
atoms.rationale: Inequalities are the most common mathematical constraint; ambiguous chained comparison is a real parsing hazard.

atoms.name: ordinals and transfinite indexing
atoms.essential_semantics: Well-ordered indices beyond the naturals supporting transfinite induction.
atoms.canonical_example: the Borel hierarchy indexed by countable ordinals
atoms.rationale: Rarely needed outside set theory and descriptive set theory, but the natural completion of the indexing story.

atoms.name: p-adic and alternative completions
atoms.essential_semantics: A completion of Q under a non-archimedean absolute value, with its own notion of nearness.
atoms.canonical_example: |p^n|_p = p^{-n} tends to 0
atoms.rationale: Included as a deliberate low-weight probe of whether 'the reals' are hard-wired as the only completion.

atoms.name: strictly positive reals
atoms.essential_semantics: Refinement by x > 0, closed under multiplication and division; the domain on which log is total.
atoms.canonical_example: sigma > 0 as a scale parameter
atoms.rationale: Scale parameters, rates and bandwidths are strictly positive; the strict/non-strict distinction changes which operations are total.

atoms.name: primality
atoms.essential_semantics: A predicate on integers with the standard definition, usable inside quantified statements.
atoms.canonical_example: there are infinitely many primes
atoms.rationale: The canonical test of whether a predicate can be defined and quantified over an infinite discrete domain.

atoms.name: probability-valued scalar distinct from generic magnitude
atoms.essential_semantics: A value carrying the semantics of a probability (normalisation, complement, product-under-independence) rather than merely a number in [0,1].
atoms.canonical_example: P(A) = 0.3, hence P(A^c) = 0.7
atoms.rationale: A probability and a positive magnitude are not interchangeable even when numerically equal; the complement operation is meaningful for one and not the other.

atoms.name: quaternions and non-commutative scalars
atoms.essential_semantics: A scalar-like domain where multiplication is not commutative, forcing the representation to respect operand order.
atoms.canonical_example: ij = k but ji = -k
atoms.rationale: A cheap stress test for whether the system assumes commutativity of multiplication everywhere.

atoms.name: rationals
atoms.essential_semantics: Field of exact fractions, with equality up to reduction, not represented as a float.
atoms.canonical_example: 1/3 in Q, and 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 exactly
atoms.rationale: The exact/inexact boundary is where most mathematical software silently lies; rationals are the canonical exact non-integer domain.

atoms.name: real numbers
atoms.essential_semantics: Complete ordered field treated as an idealised mathematical object, explicitly distinct from any floating-point approximation of it.
atoms.canonical_example: pi in R
atoms.rationale: Almost all analysis, probability and physics is stated over R; identifying R with float64 is a category error with measurable consequences.

atoms.name: sign function and signed reasoning
atoms.essential_semantics: A three-valued sign with sign(0) defined by convention, and sign-based case reasoning.
atoms.canonical_example: sign(x) * |x| = x
atoms.rationale: Small but a common source of convention drift at zero, which a representation should pin down.

atoms.name: named mathematical constants
atoms.essential_semantics: pi, e, gamma etc. as exact symbolic constants, not as their decimal approximations.
atoms.canonical_example: integral over R of e^{-x^2} dx = sqrt(pi)
atoms.rationale: Closed-form results are stated with symbolic constants; substituting decimals loses exactness and blocks symbolic simplification.

atoms.name: unit interval [0,1]
atoms.essential_semantics: Refinement of R to [0,1], closed under multiplication and convex combination but not under addition.
atoms.canonical_example: p in [0,1] as a Bernoulli parameter
atoms.rationale: Probabilities and mixture weights live here; a type that permits p1 + p2 to escape [0,1] without comment is unsound for probability.

atoms.name: numeric vector with declared length
atoms.essential_semantics: A finite indexed tuple of scalars whose length is part of its type and whose element type is uniform.
atoms.canonical_example: x in R^n
atoms.rationale: Parameter vectors, data points and decision variables are all length-typed vectors; untyped lists lose conformability.

atoms.name: basis and change of coordinates
atoms.essential_semantics: Explicit basis objects and similarity transformations, with invariants marked as basis-independent.
atoms.rationale: Coordinate-dependence is a real property of statements; a representation that cannot mention the basis cannot express it.

atoms.name: elementwise operations and broadcasting rules
atoms.essential_semantics: Elementwise application is distinguished from algebraic operations, and any shape-broadcasting rule is explicit and checkable.
atoms.canonical_example: A * B (matrix product) versus A .* B (elementwise)
atoms.rationale: The elementwise/algebraic overload of '*' is a notorious ambiguity with silent numerical consequences.

atoms.name: category, objects and morphisms
atoms.essential_semantics: Objects with composable morphisms, identities and associativity, permitting structural statements independent of elements.
atoms.canonical_example: Vect_k with linear maps as morphisms
atoms.rationale: Rarely necessary for applied work; included to mark the upper boundary of algebraic abstraction rather than to be expected.

atoms.name: determinant
atoms.essential_semantics: Scalar invariant of a square matrix with multiplicativity and its volume interpretation available.
atoms.canonical_example: det(AB) = det(A) det(B)
atoms.rationale: It links invertibility, orientation and change-of-variables; its absence blocks the Jacobian rule for densities.

atoms.name: dual space and covectors
atoms.essential_semantics: Linear functionals as objects, with the row/column and vector/covector distinction maintained.
atoms.canonical_example: gradient as a covector acting on tangent vectors
atoms.rationale: The gradient-as-covector distinction matters in geometry and in correctly typed automatic differentiation.

atoms.name: eigenvalues and eigenvectors
atoms.essential_semantics: Solutions of Av = lambda v with multiplicity and the possibility of complex eigenvalues for real matrices.
atoms.canonical_example: A v = lambda v, v != 0
atoms.rationale: Spectral statements pervade dynamics, statistics and physics; the excluded v != 0 condition is routinely dropped.

atoms.name: implicit summation convention
atoms.essential_semantics: A convention where repeated indices are summed, with the convention explicitly declared rather than assumed.
atoms.canonical_example: v^i w_i denotes sum_i v^i w_i
atoms.rationale: Convenience notation whose implicitness is exactly the kind of ambiguity a formal IR should make explicit.

atoms.name: equation as a stated relation between terms
atoms.essential_semantics: An assertion of equality between two terms with a declared unknown, which is a proposition and not an assignment.
atoms.rationale: Equations are the primary objects of algebra; representing them as assignment statements loses their propositional character.

atoms.name: polynomial factorisation and roots
atoms.essential_semantics: Factoring relative to a declared ground field, with multiplicity of roots recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: x^2 + 1 is irreducible over R but factors over C
atoms.rationale: Field-relativity of factorisation is a good test of whether the ground structure is tracked.

atoms.name: field
atoms.essential_semantics: A commutative ring where every nonzero element is invertible; the ground structure over which vector spaces are defined.
atoms.canonical_example: R and C are fields; Z is not
atoms.rationale: Linear algebra statements are parameterised by the ground field; hard-wiring R is an unrecorded restriction.

atoms.name: functorial construction
atoms.essential_semantics: A construction acting on both objects and morphisms while preserving composition.
atoms.canonical_example: the pushforward of a measure along a measurable map
atoms.rationale: Included because the probabilistic pushforward is exactly a functorial action and is often represented as an ad hoc special case.

atoms.name: presentation by generators and relations
atoms.essential_semantics: A structure specified by generating elements plus imposed identities.
atoms.canonical_example: the cyclic group <g | g^n = e>
atoms.rationale: The standard finite description of infinite structures; tests whether definitions may be given by constraint rather than construction.

atoms.name: group
atoms.essential_semantics: A set with an associative operation, identity and inverses, whose axioms are stated and whose commutativity is declared not assumed.
atoms.canonical_example: (Z, +) is an abelian group
atoms.rationale: The minimal algebraic structure; whether a system can state axioms abstractly rather than only instantiate them is a real capability boundary.

atoms.name: structure-preserving map
atoms.essential_semantics: A map between structures with the preservation conditions stated, so that 'is a homomorphism' is a checkable property.
atoms.rationale: Preservation properties are the content of algebra; a map with no declared structure is just a function.

atoms.name: ideal
atoms.essential_semantics: Absorbing subring used to form quotients and to state algebraic-geometry correspondences.
atoms.canonical_example: the ideal generated by x^2 - 2 in Q[x]
atoms.rationale: Needed for symbolic algebra (Groebner bases, elimination) rather than everyday modelling.

atoms.name: inequality as a stated relation
atoms.essential_semantics: Strict and non-strict order assertions over an ordered domain, combinable and negatable.
atoms.canonical_example: x^2 >= 0 for all real x
atoms.rationale: Bounds and constraints are inequalities; the strict/non-strict distinction determines whether optima are attained.

atoms.name: inner product and orthogonality
atoms.essential_semantics: Bilinear (or sesquilinear) positive-definite form inducing angle and orthogonality.
atoms.canonical_example: <u, v> = 0 means u is orthogonal to v
atoms.rationale: Projection, least squares and Hilbert-space arguments all rest on it; conjugate-linearity in the complex case is easily got wrong.

atoms.name: matrix inverse with invertibility obligation
atoms.essential_semantics: Defined only for square non-singular matrices; using it emits an invertibility side condition.
atoms.canonical_example: x = A^{-1} b requires det(A) != 0
atoms.rationale: Silent inversion of a singular or ill-conditioned matrix is a canonical authoritative-looking-but-wrong output.

atoms.name: isomorphism and structural identity
atoms.essential_semantics: Invertible structure-preserving map; 'isomorphic' is distinguished from 'equal'.
atoms.canonical_example: every n-dimensional real vector space is isomorphic to R^n but not equal to it
atoms.rationale: Identifying isomorphic-with-equal is the standard way structure-preserving-but-lossy translations are mis-sold as faithful.

atoms.name: kernel, image, rank-nullity
atoms.essential_semantics: Subobjects induced by a map, with the dimension relation statable.
atoms.canonical_example: dim ker T + dim im T = dim V
atoms.rationale: Solvability of linear systems is a kernel/image statement; without it solvability can only be tested numerically.

atoms.name: outer, Kronecker and tensor products
atoms.essential_semantics: Shape-multiplying products distinguished from inner products, with resulting shape derivable.
atoms.canonical_example: u v^T in R^{m x n} from u in R^m, v in R^n
atoms.rationale: Covariance structures and multi-way models are built from these; confusing them with inner products is a shape error.

atoms.name: linear map distinct from its matrix
atoms.essential_semantics: A basis-independent map, with a matrix being its representation in chosen bases.
atoms.canonical_example: T : V -> W with [T]_{B,C} its matrix in bases B, C
atoms.rationale: One semantic object with many matrix views; collapsing map and matrix loses basis-dependence information.

atoms.name: matrix as a typed object
atoms.essential_semantics: A rectangular array over a ring whose row and column counts are part of its type and whose entries are addressable.
atoms.canonical_example: A in R^{m x n}
atoms.rationale: Linear algebra is the working language of applied mathematics; a matrix without shape typing cannot support conformability checking.

atoms.name: matrix addition and non-commutative multiplication
atoms.essential_semantics: Multiplication is associative but not commutative and operand order is preserved through all transformations.
atoms.canonical_example: AB != BA in general
atoms.rationale: Any canonicaliser that sorts operands commutatively will silently produce false matrix identities; this is a testable failure.

atoms.name: factorisations (LU, QR, Cholesky, SVD, spectral)
atoms.essential_semantics: Existence conditions and uniqueness conventions are part of the statement, not implementation details.
atoms.canonical_example: A = L L^T requires A symmetric positive definite
atoms.rationale: Decompositions carry preconditions; hiding them in a backend call is exactly the silent-loss failure mode.

atoms.name: shape conformability checking
atoms.essential_semantics: Operations reject non-conformable operands statically, and shape variables may be symbolic (m, n rather than literals).
atoms.canonical_example: A in R^{2x3}, B in R^{4x5}: AB is rejected
atoms.rationale: Shape errors are the dominant error class in numerical code; catching them is a primary reason to have a typed mathematical IR.

atoms.name: module over a ring
atoms.essential_semantics: Generalisation of a vector space where scalars form a ring, so bases need not exist.
atoms.canonical_example: Z^n as a Z-module
atoms.rationale: Low practical frequency, but tests whether 'vector space' was implemented as a special case or hard-coded.

atoms.name: norm on a vector space
atoms.essential_semantics: Non-negative, homogeneous, subadditive functional with the specific norm identified (which p, which matrix norm).
atoms.canonical_example: ||x||_2 = sqrt(sum x_i^2)
atoms.rationale: Unspecified 'norm' in an error bound or regulariser makes the statement meaningless; the index is semantic content.

atoms.name: ordered algebraic structure
atoms.essential_semantics: Structures where an order interacts with operations (ordered field, positive cone), with compatibility axioms stated.
atoms.canonical_example: a <= b implies a + c <= b + c
atoms.rationale: Inequality manipulation rules depend on order-operation compatibility, which is often assumed silently and wrongly (e.g. multiplying by a negative).

atoms.name: polynomial as a structured object
atoms.essential_semantics: A polynomial has an identifiable indeterminate, degree and coefficients, and is not merely an opaque expression tree.
atoms.rationale: Degree and coefficient extraction are semantic operations; a representation that cannot answer 'what is the degree' does not really have polynomials.

atoms.name: positive (semi-)definiteness
atoms.essential_semantics: The property x^T A x > 0 (or >= 0) for all nonzero x, as a type-level constraint with its own quantified definition.
atoms.canonical_example: Sigma is a covariance matrix, hence symmetric positive semidefinite
atoms.rationale: Covariance matrices and convex quadratics are defined by this property; a system that treats a covariance as an arbitrary matrix admits impossible models.

atoms.name: quotient structure
atoms.essential_semantics: Structure induced on equivalence classes, with well-definedness of induced operations required.
atoms.canonical_example: R/I as a quotient ring
atoms.rationale: The general form of modular arithmetic and of function spaces modulo null sets.

atoms.name: rank
atoms.essential_semantics: Dimension of the image, connecting to solvability and identifiability.
atoms.canonical_example: rank(X) = p means the design matrix has full column rank
atoms.rationale: Statistical identifiability is a rank condition; without rank it can only be diagnosed numerically.

atoms.name: rational function with pole structure
atoms.essential_semantics: Quotient of polynomials carrying its domain of definition (poles excluded) rather than being assumed total.
atoms.canonical_example: f(x) = (x+1)/(x-2), defined for x != 2
atoms.rationale: Poles are the standard case where simplification (cancelling a factor) changes the domain, a classic soundness trap.

atoms.name: ring
atoms.essential_semantics: Two operations with distributivity, with commutativity and unity declared explicitly.
atoms.canonical_example: Z is a commutative ring with unity
atoms.rationale: Polynomials and matrices are ring-valued; keeping the abstraction lets shared theorems be stated once.

atoms.name: solution set as an object
atoms.essential_semantics: The set of assignments satisfying a system, which may be empty, finite, or a manifold, and is distinguishable from a single returned root.
atoms.canonical_example: { (x,y) : x^2 + y^2 = 1 } is a circle, not a number
atoms.rationale: Returning 'the solution' when there are zero or infinitely many is a common and consequential misrepresentation.

atoms.name: substructure (subgroup, subspace, subring)
atoms.essential_semantics: A subset closed under the operations, with closure as a checkable condition.
atoms.canonical_example: the set of symmetric matrices is a subspace of all matrices
atoms.rationale: Closure conditions are where many modelling errors live; making them explicit makes them checkable.

atoms.name: algebraic simplification with side conditions
atoms.essential_semantics: Rewriting an expression to an equivalent one, with domain-narrowing steps flagged (cancelling requires nonzero, sqrt(x^2)=|x|).
atoms.canonical_example: (x^2-1)/(x-1) simplifies to x+1 only for x != 1
atoms.rationale: Unconditioned simplification is the classic way a symbolic system produces a subtly false identity.

atoms.name: unbound symbolic variable / indeterminate
atoms.essential_semantics: A named symbol that denotes an unknown of a declared domain and can be manipulated without a value being supplied.
atoms.canonical_example: solve x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 for x
atoms.rationale: Symbolic mathematics begins with symbols that have types but no values; languages that require every name to be bound to a value cannot do algebra.

atoms.name: structured matrix classes
atoms.essential_semantics: Symmetric, Hermitian, orthogonal, unitary, triangular, diagonal, sparse as type-level properties preserved or lost by operations.
atoms.canonical_example: Q^T Q = I characterises orthogonal Q
atoms.rationale: Structure determines which algorithms and theorems apply; if structure is not in the type it must be rechecked or assumed.

atoms.name: simultaneous system of equations/inequalities
atoms.essential_semantics: A conjunctive collection of relations sharing unknowns, treated as one object with a joint solution set.
atoms.canonical_example: Ax = b together with x >= 0
atoms.rationale: Systems, not single equations, are the unit of linear algebra and optimisation modelling.

atoms.name: tensor with declared rank and shape
atoms.essential_semantics: Multi-index array with rank, per-axis dimensions, and (where relevant) variance of indices in its type.
atoms.canonical_example: T in R^{n1 x n2 x n3}
atoms.rationale: Modern applied mathematics and physics are tensor-valued; degrading tensors to nested lists loses axis semantics.

atoms.name: named index notation with binding
atoms.essential_semantics: Indices are bound names with declared ranges; repeated indices are distinguishable as bound (summed) or free.
atoms.canonical_example: C_{ik} = sum_j A_{ij} B_{jk}
atoms.rationale: Index notation is a binding construct; representing indices as mere integers loses which are contracted.

atoms.name: trace
atoms.essential_semantics: Linear invariant with the cyclic property, basis independent.
atoms.canonical_example: tr(AB) = tr(BA)
atoms.rationale: Frequently used in statistics (degrees of freedom, covariance) and a good test of invariant reasoning.

atoms.name: transpose and conjugate transpose
atoms.essential_semantics: Shape-reversing involution, with the real transpose and complex adjoint distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: (AB)^T = B^T A^T
atoms.rationale: Order reversal under transposition is a standard identity that a commutativity-assuming system gets wrong.

atoms.name: vector space over a field
atoms.essential_semantics: Abelian group with scalar action, with the field, dimension and basis-independence expressible.
atoms.canonical_example: R^n is an n-dimensional real vector space
atoms.rationale: The setting for linear algebra, functional analysis and geometry; conflating a vector space with an array of numbers loses basis independence.

atoms.name: almost-everywhere / almost-sure qualification
atoms.essential_semantics: A property holding outside a null set, with the qualification attached to the statement rather than dropped.
atoms.canonical_example: f = g almost everywhere with respect to Lebesgue measure
atoms.rationale: The difference between 'everywhere' and 'almost everywhere' is a genuine weakening; a system that drops the qualifier overstates the claim.

atoms.name: asymptotic order notation
atoms.essential_semantics: Big-O, little-o, Theta and asymptotic equivalence with the limit point and the variable made explicit; O(.) is a relation, not a value.
atoms.canonical_example: f(n) = O(n log n) as n -> infinity
atoms.rationale: The '=' in O-notation is not equality; representing it as such licenses invalid symmetric reasoning.

atoms.name: boundary condition with type
atoms.essential_semantics: Dirichlet, Neumann, Robin and periodic conditions distinguished, attached to a specified part of the boundary.
atoms.canonical_example: u = 0 on the boundary (Dirichlet)
atoms.rationale: Boundary-condition type determines solution existence and uniqueness; an untyped 'boundary value' is insufficient.

atoms.name: composition and the chain rule
atoms.essential_semantics: Differentiation of composed maps respecting order and shapes, including the matrix-product form in the multivariate case.
atoms.canonical_example: D(g o f)(x) = Dg(f(x)) Df(x)
atoms.rationale: Backpropagation and change-of-variables are the chain rule; the non-commutative product order is where implementations go wrong.

atoms.name: holomorphy, poles and residues
atoms.essential_semantics: Complex differentiability with singularity classification and contour integration.
atoms.canonical_example: residue of 1/(z^2+1) at z = i
atoms.rationale: Characteristic functions and transform inversion rely on complex analysis; without it those results are opaque.

atoms.name: continuity at a point and on a set
atoms.essential_semantics: Pointwise continuity and continuity on a set are distinct claims, each with an explicit domain.
atoms.canonical_example: f is continuous on [a, b]
atoms.rationale: Continuity is the most common hypothesis in analysis theorems; it is a property of a function-on-a-domain, not of a formula.

atoms.name: distinct modes of convergence
atoms.essential_semantics: Pointwise, uniform, L^p, almost-everywhere convergence are separate relations and must not be merged into a single 'converges'.
atoms.canonical_example: f_n -> f in L^2 but not pointwise
atoms.rationale: Different modes support different theorems; collapsing them is a substantive semantic loss with practical consequences.

atoms.name: convolution
atoms.essential_semantics: A binary operation on functions or measures with its own domain conditions, distinguished from pointwise product.
atoms.canonical_example: (f * g)(x) = integral f(y) g(x - y) dy
atoms.rationale: The distribution of a sum of independent random variables is a convolution; representing it as multiplication is wrong.

atoms.name: derivative with respect to a named variable
atoms.essential_semantics: The differentiation variable is explicit, the point of evaluation is distinguished from the derivative function, and differentiability is a claim with a domain.
atoms.canonical_example: f'(x) = df/dx, and f'(2) evaluated at a point
atoms.rationale: Differentiation is the central operator of applied mathematics, and the derivative-as-function versus derivative-at-a-point distinction is frequently collapsed.

atoms.name: directional and total derivative
atoms.essential_semantics: Derivative along a direction, and the total (Frechet) derivative as a linear map, distinguished from the collection of partials.
atoms.canonical_example: D_v f(x) = lim_{t->0} (f(x + tv) - f(x))/t
atoms.rationale: Existence of all partials does not imply differentiability; systems that identify them are stating something false.

atoms.name: explicit domain and codomain of a function
atoms.essential_semantics: A function carries its source and target sets as part of its identity; two formulas with the same rule but different domains are different functions.
atoms.rationale: Nearly every analytic theorem has a domain hypothesis; a function represented only by its rule cannot satisfy or violate it.

atoms.name: fixed points and contraction
atoms.essential_semantics: Solutions of x = T(x) with contraction or compactness hypotheses making existence a theorem rather than an assumption.
atoms.canonical_example: a contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point
atoms.rationale: Equilibrium concepts and iterative schemes are fixed-point statements; the hypotheses are what make them valid.

atoms.name: derivative with respect to a function
atoms.essential_semantics: Variation of a functional with respect to its function argument, distinguished from partials with respect to scalars.
atoms.canonical_example: delta S / delta y for an action functional S[y]
atoms.rationale: Calculus of variations, physics and variational inference all differentiate with respect to functions, not numbers.

atoms.name: real- and vector-valued functions
atoms.essential_semantics: Scalar, vector and matrix valued functions of one or several variables, with arity and value type distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: F : R^n -> R^m
atoms.rationale: The multivariate/multivalued shape determines which derivative object (gradient, Jacobian, Hessian) is meaningful.

atoms.name: function spaces as typed objects
atoms.essential_semantics: L^p, C^k, Sobolev and Hilbert spaces as types with their norm and equivalence relation, so membership is a checkable hypothesis.
atoms.rationale: Statements in functional analysis, signal processing and nonparametric statistics quantify over function spaces.

atoms.name: generalized functions / Schwartz distributions
atoms.essential_semantics: Objects such as the Dirac delta defined by their action on test functions, and explicitly not ordinary functions.
atoms.canonical_example: integral delta(x) phi(x) dx = phi(0)
atoms.rationale: Included partly because 'distribution' is dangerously overloaded between analysis and probability; a good IR keeps them distinct.

atoms.name: gradient
atoms.essential_semantics: Vector (or covector) of partials with shape determined by the domain, and its distinction from the total derivative recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: grad f(x) in R^n for f : R^n -> R
atoms.rationale: Optimisation and learning are gradient-driven; shape and variance errors here propagate silently.

atoms.name: Hessian and second-order structure
atoms.essential_semantics: Matrix of second partials, symmetric under continuity hypotheses, connected to convexity and to optimality conditions.
atoms.canonical_example: H f(x) positive semidefinite characterises local convexity
atoms.rationale: Second-order conditions and Fisher information are Hessians; symmetry requires a hypothesis that should not be assumed silently.

atoms.name: higher-order derivatives and smoothness classes
atoms.essential_semantics: Derivatives of order k with C^k / C^infinity / analytic smoothness classes as hypotheses.
atoms.canonical_example: f in C^2([a,b])
atoms.rationale: Smoothness class is the hypothesis of most approximation theorems; treating 'differentiable' as a Boolean loses the order.

atoms.name: implicit function and implicit differentiation
atoms.essential_semantics: Derivatives of a relation-defined function, with the non-degeneracy condition of the implicit function theorem attached.
atoms.canonical_example: from x^2 + y^2 = 1, dy/dx = -x/y for y != 0
atoms.rationale: Constrained sensitivity analysis relies on it, and its side condition is exactly the sort of thing routinely dropped.

atoms.name: improper integrals and convergence conditions
atoms.essential_semantics: Integrals over unbounded domains or of unbounded integrands are limits, whose existence is a claim.
atoms.canonical_example: integral from 1 to infinity of 1/x^2 dx converges; of 1/x diverges
atoms.rationale: Normalisability of densities and existence of moments are improper-integral convergence claims.

atoms.name: initial condition
atoms.essential_semantics: Value of the unknown (and derivatives) at a specified point, attached to the differential equation as part of one problem object.
atoms.rationale: Without initial data the solution is a family; conflating the equation with the initial-value problem loses well-posedness.

atoms.name: definite integral with explicit variable and domain
atoms.essential_semantics: Integration binds a variable, carries an explicit domain and an explicit measure/differential; the bound variable does not escape.
atoms.canonical_example: integral from 0 to 1 of x^2 dx
atoms.rationale: Integration is a binder with a domain and a measure; representations that keep only the integrand lose most of the statement.

atoms.name: antiderivative and constant of integration
atoms.essential_semantics: The antiderivative is a family of functions differing by a constant, not a single function.
atoms.canonical_example: integral of 2x dx = x^2 + C
atoms.rationale: Dropping the constant of integration is a small but real loss of the solution family.

atoms.name: integration against a general measure
atoms.essential_semantics: Integral of a measurable function with respect to a named measure, unifying sums and Riemann integrals.
atoms.canonical_example: integral of f dmu over A
atoms.rationale: It is the construct that lets discrete and continuous cases share one statement; without it they must be duplicated.

atoms.name: Jacobian matrix
atoms.essential_semantics: Matrix of first partials of a vector-valued function with shape m x n determined by the types.
atoms.canonical_example: J_F(x) in R^{m x n} for F : R^n -> R^m
atoms.rationale: Change of variables for densities and the multivariate chain rule both require the Jacobian with correct orientation.

atoms.name: limit of a function at a point
atoms.essential_semantics: A limit is a quantified statement (for all epsilon there exists delta), not an evaluation; one-sided limits are distinguished and existence is a claim.
atoms.canonical_example: lim_{x -> 0} sin(x)/x = 1
atoms.rationale: The limit is the founding construct of analysis and the canonical alternating-quantifier statement; systems that treat it as a numeric operation lose the claim structure.

atoms.name: limit of a sequence, including limits at infinity
atoms.essential_semantics: Convergence of an indexed family as n tends to infinity, with divergence and oscillation distinguishable from convergence.
atoms.canonical_example: lim_{n -> infinity} (1 + 1/n)^n = e
atoms.rationale: Asymptotic statements in probability and numerics are sequence limits; the index domain and the mode of convergence are semantic content.

atoms.name: integration over curves and surfaces
atoms.essential_semantics: Integration along a parameterised curve or over an embedded surface with orientation recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: line integral of F . dr along a closed curve C
atoms.rationale: Vector calculus and physics need orientation-aware integration, which a plain domain-integral cannot express.

atoms.name: measurable function
atoms.essential_semantics: Preimages of measurable sets are measurable; measurability is a hypothesis attached to a function and a pair of sigma-algebras.
atoms.canonical_example: X : Omega -> R is F/Borel measurable
atoms.rationale: A random variable IS a measurable function; systems that define random variables purely by their distribution cannot state measurability.

atoms.name: measure
atoms.essential_semantics: A countably additive non-negative set function on a sigma-algebra, with the reference measure of an integral nameable.
atoms.canonical_example: Lebesgue measure on R; counting measure on N
atoms.rationale: Densities are densities with respect to a measure; suppressing the reference measure makes discrete/continuous unification impossible.

atoms.name: metric and metric-space structure
atoms.essential_semantics: A distance function with its axioms, generalising absolute value, and the induced notions of ball and convergence.
atoms.canonical_example: d(x,y) = |x - y| on R
atoms.rationale: Convergence and continuity outside R^n need an explicit metric; assuming Euclidean distance is an unrecorded commitment.

atoms.name: monotonicity, boundedness and convexity of functions
atoms.essential_semantics: Qualitative function properties as stated, checkable predicates with a domain.
atoms.canonical_example: f is non-decreasing on [0, infinity)
atoms.rationale: CDFs, utility functions and objectives are characterised by such properties; they are part of the mathematical content, not metadata.

atoms.name: iterated and multiple integration
atoms.essential_semantics: Integration over multidimensional regions with the region description and the order of integration explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: double integral over the unit disc of f(x,y) dA
atoms.rationale: Marginalisation is a multiple integral; the region and integration order carry Fubini-type side conditions.

atoms.name: ordinary differential equation
atoms.essential_semantics: A relation among a function and its derivatives with the independent variable, the unknown function and the order identified.
atoms.canonical_example: y'' + omega^2 y = 0
atoms.rationale: Dynamics is expressed as differential equations; the unknown being a function rather than a number is the key typing fact.

atoms.name: partial derivative with held-constant variables
atoms.essential_semantics: Which variables are held fixed is part of the meaning, not a convention; the same symbol can denote different partials under different variable sets.
atoms.canonical_example: (partial f / partial x) at fixed y
atoms.rationale: In thermodynamics and economics the held-constant set is written explicitly precisely because omitting it changes the quantity.

atoms.name: partial function with restricted domain
atoms.essential_semantics: A function defined on a subset of its nominal source, with the definedness set recoverable.
atoms.canonical_example: log : R -> R defined only on x > 0
atoms.rationale: Partiality is not an error condition, it is part of the mathematics; systems that model it only as a runtime exception lose it from the statement.

atoms.name: partial differential equation
atoms.essential_semantics: Relation among partial derivatives of a multivariate unknown function, with the independent variables and domain explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: u_t = alpha u_xx on (0, L) x (0, T)
atoms.rationale: The spatial domain and boundary data are as much a part of the problem as the equation; keeping only the equation is a lossy representation.

atoms.name: piecewise definition over a partition of the domain
atoms.essential_semantics: A function defined by cases with guards, where exhaustiveness and mutual exclusivity of the cases are checkable and the pieces' domains are explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: f(x) = x for x >= 0, -x for x < 0
atoms.rationale: Piecewise objects are ubiquitous (densities, activation functions, tariffs); overlapping or non-exhaustive cases are silent errors.

atoms.name: power series and radius of convergence
atoms.essential_semantics: Series in powers of (x - a) with a centre and a radius of convergence carried with it.
atoms.canonical_example: sum x^n/n! with infinite radius of convergence
atoms.rationale: A series expansion without its region of validity is a common source of misuse outside the radius.

atoms.name: infinite series and convergence
atoms.essential_semantics: An infinite sum is a limit of partial sums; convergence, absolute convergence and conditional convergence are distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: sum_{n=1}^{infinity} 1/n^2 = pi^2/6
atoms.rationale: Rearrangement is invalid for conditionally convergent series; a representation that treats infinite sums as finite ones is unsound.

atoms.name: sigma-algebra of measurable sets
atoms.essential_semantics: A collection closed under complement and countable union, usable as an object (for conditioning, filtrations, measurability).
atoms.canonical_example: the Borel sigma-algebra on R
atoms.rationale: Conditioning on a sigma-algebra and information filtrations are inexpressible without it; this is a hard boundary for probabilistic IRs.

atoms.name: named special functions with branch and domain data
atoms.essential_semantics: Gamma, Beta, Bessel, erf, log with their domains, poles and branch cuts recorded rather than assumed.
atoms.canonical_example: Gamma(n) = (n-1)! for positive integers, with poles at non-positive integers
atoms.rationale: Normalising constants of standard distributions are special functions; branch and domain data is real semantic content.

atoms.name: supremum and infimum versus maximum and minimum
atoms.essential_semantics: Least upper bound of a set, possibly not attained and possibly infinite, distinguished from a maximum.
atoms.canonical_example: sup of (0,1) is 1 but has no maximum
atoms.rationale: Optimisation statements that say 'min' where only 'inf' is justified assert attainment that may be false.

atoms.name: Taylor expansion with remainder
atoms.essential_semantics: Finite expansion plus an explicit remainder or error term, not an unqualified equality.
atoms.rationale: Writing a truncated expansion with '=' rather than '≈ with remainder R' is a textbook example of dropped semantics.

atoms.name: integral transforms
atoms.essential_semantics: Fourier, Laplace, Mellin and related transforms as operators on functions, with the convention (sign, 2 pi placement) recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: F(omega) = integral f(t) e^{-i omega t} dt
atoms.rationale: Transform conventions differ across fields; an unrecorded convention makes results incomparable.

atoms.name: uniform continuity and uniform convergence
atoms.essential_semantics: Uniformity is expressed by the position of the existential quantifier relative to the universal one and must be preserved distinctly from the pointwise version.
atoms.canonical_example: for all eps exists delta for all x versus for all x for all eps exists delta
atoms.rationale: This is the sharpest practical test of quantifier-order fidelity: the two statements differ only in binder order and are genuinely different theorems.

atoms.name: variational / stationarity problem over functions
atoms.essential_semantics: Extremising a functional over an admissible class of functions with the class stated.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise integral of L(y, y') dx over y with y(a)=A, y(b)=B
atoms.rationale: The admissible class is where the boundary conditions and regularity live; dropping it makes the problem ill-posed.

atoms.name: arithmetic on random variables preserving dependence
atoms.essential_semantics: X + Y is a random variable on the same space whose law depends on the joint law, not merely on the marginals.
atoms.canonical_example: Var(X + Y) = Var X + Var Y + 2 Cov(X, Y)
atoms.rationale: Systems that implement X + Y by convolving marginals have silently assumed independence, a common and serious error.

atoms.name: Bayes rule as a relation among distributions
atoms.essential_semantics: Posterior proportional to likelihood times prior, with the normalising constant and its existence acknowledged.
atoms.canonical_example: p(theta | x) = p(x | theta) p(theta) / p(x)
atoms.rationale: It is the inference rule of Bayesian statistics and requires distinguishing the four distinct distributions involved.

atoms.name: cumulative distribution function
atoms.essential_semantics: Right-continuous non-decreasing function with limits 0 and 1, defined for all distributions including mixed ones.
atoms.canonical_example: F_X(t) = P(X <= t)
atoms.rationale: The CDF is the representation that works uniformly across discrete, continuous and mixed distributions.

atoms.name: density transformation with Jacobian
atoms.essential_semantics: Density of a transformed variable includes the absolute Jacobian determinant and requires the transform to be a diffeomorphism.
atoms.rationale: Omitting the Jacobian is a well-known and silent source of incorrect posteriors.

atoms.name: central limit theorem and asymptotic normality
atoms.essential_semantics: Convergence in distribution of a normalised sum, with the normalisation and finite-variance hypothesis explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: sqrt(n)(Xbar - mu)/sigma converges in distribution to Normal(0,1)
atoms.rationale: Most frequentist intervals are CLT-based approximations; representing them as exact drops the asymptotic qualifier.

atoms.name: conditional distribution given a random variable
atoms.essential_semantics: A distribution-valued function of the conditioning variable (a Markov kernel), not a single distribution.
atoms.canonical_example: Y | X = x ~ Normal(beta x, sigma^2)
atoms.rationale: Every regression and hierarchical model is a conditional distribution; representing it as a distribution with a parameter that happens to mention x loses the kernel structure.

atoms.name: conditional expectation as a random variable
atoms.essential_semantics: E[Y | X] is itself a random variable (a function of X), not a number; the tower property is statable.
atoms.canonical_example: E[E[Y | X]] = E[Y]
atoms.rationale: The random-variable nature of conditional expectation is what makes the tower property and regression functions meaningful.

atoms.name: conditional independence
atoms.essential_semantics: X independent of Y given Z, a ternary relation that neither implies nor is implied by marginal independence.
atoms.canonical_example: X ⟂ Y | Z
atoms.rationale: Graphical models, causal inference and Markov structure are all conditional-independence statements; it is irreducibly ternary.

atoms.name: conditional probability given an event
atoms.essential_semantics: P(A | B) defined for P(B) > 0, with the positivity condition attached and the asymmetry of conditioning preserved.
atoms.canonical_example: P(A | B) = P(A intersect B) / P(B)
atoms.rationale: Conditioning is asymmetric and partial; both facts are frequently lost, producing the classic base-rate and inverse-probability errors.

atoms.name: conditioning on a sigma-algebra
atoms.essential_semantics: Conditional expectation given a sub-sigma-algebra, defined almost surely and characterised by a projection property rather than by a formula.
atoms.canonical_example: E[X | G] is G-measurable and integrates to E[X] over every G-set
atoms.rationale: This is the general form of conditioning that handles conditioning on probability-zero events; its absence caps a system's probabilistic expressiveness.

atoms.name: modes of stochastic convergence
atoms.essential_semantics: Almost sure, in probability, in L^p and in distribution are distinct relations with a strict implication ordering.
atoms.canonical_example: convergence in probability does not imply almost sure convergence
atoms.rationale: Asymptotic statistical guarantees are stated in a specific mode; substituting one for another changes what is guaranteed.

atoms.name: copula / separation of marginals from dependence
atoms.essential_semantics: Representation of a joint law as marginals plus a dependence structure on the unit cube.
atoms.canonical_example: F(x,y) = C(F_X(x), F_Y(y))
atoms.rationale: It makes explicit that marginals do not determine the joint, which is the core misconception copulas exist to correct.

atoms.name: the 'distributed as' relation
atoms.essential_semantics: A relation between a random variable and a distribution, distinct from equality, from assignment and from approximation.
atoms.canonical_example: X ~ Normal(mu, sigma^2)
atoms.rationale: Writing X = Normal(mu, sigma) instead of X ~ Normal(mu, sigma) is a type error that silently changes a distributional claim into an identity.

atoms.name: parametric family with named parameters
atoms.essential_semantics: The family name plus the parameter tuple, with the parameterisation convention explicit (variance versus standard deviation, rate versus scale).
atoms.canonical_example: Gamma(shape = 2, rate = 3) is not Gamma(shape = 2, scale = 3)
atoms.rationale: Silent parameterisation mismatch is one of the most frequent real errors in statistical software and is pure semantic loss.

atoms.name: distribution as a first-class object
atoms.essential_semantics: A distribution can be named, passed, compared, transformed and returned without any sampling occurring; it is not a value of the underlying type.
atoms.canonical_example: D := Normal(0, 1); mean(D) = 0
atoms.rationale: If Normal(0,1) evaluates to a sample rather than denoting a measure, no statement about the distribution itself can be made.

atoms.name: divergences between distributions
atoms.essential_semantics: KL, total variation, Wasserstein and similar, with asymmetry and absolute-continuity conditions explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: KL(q || p) is not KL(p || q)
atoms.rationale: Variational objectives are divergences; direction and support conditions change the optimum and are easily dropped.

atoms.name: entropy and mutual information
atoms.essential_semantics: Functionals of a distribution (not of a sample) with the base of the logarithm and reference measure declared.
atoms.canonical_example: H(X) = -sum p(x) log p(x)
atoms.rationale: Differential entropy is not invariant under reparameterisation; the reference measure is genuine semantic content.

atoms.name: event as a measurable set
atoms.essential_semantics: An event is a set of outcomes closed under the Boolean operations, distinct from a proposition about parameters and from a random variable.
atoms.rationale: P(.) takes events, not truth values; systems that pass Booleans to a probability operator have lost the event/proposition distinction.

atoms.name: exchangeability
atoms.essential_semantics: Invariance of the joint distribution under permutation of indices, weaker than i.i.d.
atoms.canonical_example: an exchangeable sequence need not be independent
atoms.rationale: It is the correct assumption behind hierarchical models; substituting i.i.d. is a strictly stronger and often false claim.

atoms.name: expectation as an integral against a distribution
atoms.essential_semantics: E[g(X)] binds X against a specified distribution; the distribution used must be explicit, and existence is a condition, not a guarantee.
atoms.canonical_example: E[X] = integral x f_X(x) dx, undefined for Cauchy
atoms.rationale: Expectation is a binder over a distribution; ambiguity about which distribution is integrated against is a major source of error in nested-expectation formulas.

atoms.name: filtration / information over time
atoms.essential_semantics: An increasing family of sigma-algebras representing accumulating information, and adaptedness of a process to it.
atoms.canonical_example: X_t is adapted to F_t
atoms.rationale: Statements about not using future information are filtration statements; without them the constraint is only a convention.

atoms.name: function whose value is a distribution (Markov kernel)
atoms.essential_semantics: A map from parameters or observations to distributions, typed as such, without collapsing to a sampled value.
atoms.canonical_example: k(x) = Normal(f(x), sigma^2)
