atoms.rationale: This is where most probabilistic programming systems collapse a distribution into a sample; the type Distribution[T] as a return type is the discriminating capability.

atoms.name: hierarchical / generative model structure
atoms.essential_semantics: A sequence of conditional statements whose dependency order is explicit and acyclic, defining a joint law by composition.
atoms.canonical_example: mu ~ Normal(0, 10); X_i | mu ~ Normal(mu, 1)
atoms.rationale: Modern Bayesian modelling is hierarchical; representing only the flat joint loses the generative structure needed for inference and criticism.

atoms.name: i.i.d. family
atoms.essential_semantics: An indexed family that is both independent and identically distributed, with the index set explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: X_1, ..., X_n i.i.d. Normal(mu, sigma^2)
atoms.rationale: The i.i.d. assumption underwrites nearly all elementary inference; it bundles two separable assumptions that should remain separable.

atoms.name: independence
atoms.essential_semantics: A property of a collection of random variables or events with respect to a specific measure; pairwise independence is distinct from mutual independence.
atoms.canonical_example: X and Y independent means P(X in A, Y in B) = P(X in A) P(Y in B)
atoms.rationale: Independence is an assumption with consequences; if it cannot be stated it will be assumed by default, which is the worst outcome.

atoms.name: indexed family of random variables
atoms.essential_semantics: A collection (X_i) over an index set where the index is a bound variable and the family is one object with a joint law.
atoms.canonical_example: (X_i)_{i=1..n} with X_i ~ Normal(mu_i, sigma^2)
atoms.rationale: Data models are families of random variables with index-dependent parameters; without indexing, only scalar toy models are expressible.

atoms.name: joint distribution of several random variables
atoms.essential_semantics: A distribution over a product space that determines all marginals but is not determined by them.
atoms.canonical_example: (X, Y) ~ MultivariateNormal(mu, Sigma)
atoms.rationale: Dependence lives only in the joint; a representation storing per-variable distributions has silently assumed independence.

atoms.name: laws of large numbers
atoms.essential_semantics: Convergence of sample averages with hypotheses (i.i.d., finite mean) and mode of convergence stated.
atoms.canonical_example: (1/n) sum X_i -> E[X] almost surely
atoms.rationale: Monte Carlo validity rests on it, and its hypotheses (finite mean) are frequently violated silently.

atoms.name: marginal distribution and marginalisation
atoms.essential_semantics: Obtained by integrating or summing out variables, with the marginalised variable identified.
atoms.canonical_example: f_X(x) = integral f_{X,Y}(x,y) dy
atoms.rationale: Marginalisation is the fundamental probabilistic inference operation and is a binder-eliminating transformation.

atoms.name: Markov property
atoms.essential_semantics: Conditional independence of the future from the past given the present, stated as a property of a process.
atoms.rationale: It is the assumption that makes dynamic programming and MCMC valid; it must be assertable and checkable, not implicit.

atoms.name: martingale property
atoms.essential_semantics: E[X_{t+1} | F_t] = X_t, requiring conditional expectation with respect to a filtration.
atoms.canonical_example: a fair game's fortune is a martingale
atoms.rationale: A compact test of whether conditional expectation on sigma-algebras is genuinely supported.

atoms.name: moment generating and characteristic functions
atoms.essential_semantics: Transforms of a distribution with their domains of existence, the characteristic function always existing and the MGF not.
atoms.canonical_example: phi_X(t) = E[e^{itX}]
atoms.rationale: The existence gap between MGF and characteristic function is a real distinction that a lossy representation would erase.

atoms.name: mixture distribution
atoms.essential_semantics: A convex combination of distributions with weights summing to one, distinguished from a sum of random variables.
atoms.canonical_example: 0.3 Normal(0,1) + 0.7 Normal(5,1)
atoms.rationale: Mixing distributions and adding random variables are different operations with different results; the notation invites confusion.

atoms.name: moments, central moments and cumulants
atoms.essential_semantics: Moments of any order with existence conditions and the raw/central/standardised distinction.
atoms.canonical_example: skewness is the third standardised moment
atoms.rationale: Method-of-moments and diagnostics depend on order and centring, which are easy to conflate.

atoms.name: semantic role of a distribution parameter
atoms.essential_semantics: Parameters carry roles (location, scale, shape, rate, degrees of freedom, concentration) with associated constraints, not merely positions.
atoms.canonical_example: in Normal(mu, sigma), mu is location and sigma > 0 is scale
atoms.rationale: Roles determine constraints and unit behaviour: a location shares units with the variate, a shape parameter is dimensionless.

atoms.name: probability density with respect to a reference measure
atoms.essential_semantics: A density is relative to a base measure and its value is not a probability; it can exceed one and carries reciprocal units of the variate.
atoms.canonical_example: f_X(x) = (1/(sigma sqrt(2 pi))) exp(-(x-mu)^2/(2 sigma^2))
atoms.rationale: Treating a density value as a probability is a standing error, and the reference measure is exactly what discrete/continuous unification needs.

atoms.name: probability mass function
atoms.essential_semantics: Point-mass function for a discrete distribution, summing to one over a countable support.
atoms.canonical_example: P(X = k) = choose(n,k) p^k (1-p)^{n-k}
atoms.rationale: P(X = x) is meaningful for discrete and zero for continuous variables; a system that offers one density concept for both is wrong for at least one.

atoms.name: probability measure and its axioms
atoms.essential_semantics: A measure with total mass 1 and countable additivity, applied to events and yielding a value in [0,1].
atoms.canonical_example: P(Omega) = 1, P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) for disjoint A, B
atoms.rationale: Normalisation and additivity are what make a probability a probability; without them any non-negative weighting looks the same.

atoms.name: probability space (Omega, F, P)
atoms.essential_semantics: The triple of sample space, sigma-algebra and probability measure is nameable, so that different random objects can be stated to live on the same space or on different ones.
atoms.canonical_example: let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space
atoms.rationale: Joint statements about several random variables presuppose a common space; without it, dependence cannot be stated at all, only assumed.

atoms.name: distribution of a transformed random variable
atoms.essential_semantics: The law of g(X) as the pushforward of the law of X, defined without reference to densities.
atoms.canonical_example: if X ~ Normal(0,1) then X^2 ~ ChiSquared(1)
atoms.rationale: Arithmetic on random variables must produce a law, not a number; this is the operation that makes X + Y meaningful.

atoms.name: quantile function / generalised inverse CDF
atoms.essential_semantics: Generalised inverse defined even when the CDF is not strictly increasing, with the convention explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: the 0.975 quantile of the standard normal is about 1.96
atoms.rationale: Interval estimates are quantile statements; ties and jumps require the generalised inverse convention to be stated.

atoms.name: random functions and function-valued distributions
atoms.essential_semantics: A distribution over a function space (e.g. a Gaussian process) where a draw is a function, not a number.
atoms.canonical_example: f ~ GP(m, k), f(x) is then a random variable for each x
atoms.rationale: Nonparametric Bayesian methods need distributions over functions; systems limited to numeric variates cannot type them.

atoms.name: matrix- and vector-valued random variables
atoms.essential_semantics: A random variable whose value space is a matrix or vector space, with shape typing and distributional constraints (e.g. Wishart yields PSD matrices) simultaneously enforced.
atoms.canonical_example: Sigma ~ InverseWishart(nu, Psi) with Sigma symmetric positive definite
atoms.rationale: This is the hardest routine composition in applied Bayesian statistics: randomness, shape and structural constraints must all hold at once.

atoms.name: random variable as an object distinct from its distribution and from its value
atoms.essential_semantics: A measurable function from the sample space to a value space; it is neither a number nor a distribution, and its identity supports dependence with other random variables.
atoms.canonical_example: X : Omega -> R with X ~ Normal(0,1)
atoms.rationale: The three-way distinction between a random variable, its distribution, and a realised value is the single most important type distinction in probabilistic modelling; collapsing any pair of them makes dependence, conditioning and pushforward inexpressible.

atoms.name: realisation / observed value of a random variable
atoms.essential_semantics: A concrete outcome value, typed as an element of the value space and distinguished from the random variable that produced it.
atoms.canonical_example: x = 1.7 is an observed value of X
atoms.rationale: The upper-case X versus lower-case x convention encodes a real type distinction that most programming representations erase.

atoms.name: stochastic process indexed by time or space
atoms.essential_semantics: A family of random variables indexed by a continuum or a discrete set, with the index set and state space distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: (W_t)_{t >= 0} standard Brownian motion
atoms.rationale: Time-series and spatial models are processes; representing them as vectors of random variables loses the continuum index.

atoms.name: stopping time
atoms.essential_semantics: A random time whose occurrence is determined by information available up to that time.
atoms.canonical_example: the first t with X_t > a is a stopping time
atoms.rationale: Optional stopping is a real inferential hazard (peeking at data); representing it requires the information structure.

atoms.name: support of a distribution
atoms.essential_semantics: The set on which the distribution places mass, part of the distribution's identity and constraining admissible observations.
atoms.canonical_example: support of Exponential is [0, infinity)
atoms.rationale: Observing a value outside the support makes the likelihood zero; a representation without support cannot detect impossible data.

atoms.name: truncation and censoring
atoms.essential_semantics: Restricting a distribution to a subset with renormalisation (truncation), versus partial observation of the value (censoring); the two are distinct.
atoms.canonical_example: X ~ Normal(0,1) truncated to x > 0
atoms.rationale: Truncation changes the distribution, censoring changes the likelihood; conflating them yields wrong inference.

atoms.name: variance, covariance and correlation
atoms.essential_semantics: Second-moment quantities with correct types (variance non-negative, covariance matrix PSD, correlation in [-1,1]) and units (squared units for variance).
atoms.canonical_example: Cov(X, Y) = E[(X - EX)(Y - EY)]
atoms.rationale: The PSD constraint on covariance matrices and the squared units of variance are both routinely violated by naive representations.

atoms.name: bias of an estimator
atoms.essential_semantics: E[estimator] - target, relative to a specified data-generating distribution.
atoms.canonical_example: the MLE of variance is biased downward by a factor (n-1)/n
atoms.rationale: Bias is defined only relative to an assumed truth; representations that omit the assumed model make it meaningless.

atoms.name: bootstrap and resampling distributions
atoms.essential_semantics: Approximating a sampling distribution by resampling, with the approximation status explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: bootstrap percentile interval for the median
atoms.rationale: The resulting interval is doubly approximate (resampling plus Monte Carlo error), which should be recorded.

atoms.name: intervention (do-operator) distinct from conditioning
atoms.essential_semantics: P(Y | do(X = x)) is not P(Y | X = x); intervention modifies the generating mechanism.
atoms.canonical_example: P(recovery | do(treatment)) versus P(recovery | treatment)
atoms.rationale: The conditioning/intervention distinction is the central formal content of causal inference and is invisible in ordinary probability notation.

atoms.name: confidence interval
atoms.essential_semantics: A random interval whose coverage probability is a property of the procedure, not of a particular realised interval.
atoms.canonical_example: P(theta in [L(X), U(X)]) = 0.95 over repeated sampling
atoms.rationale: The coverage statement quantifies over the random interval, not the parameter; systems that store only endpoints lose the quantifier structure entirely.

atoms.name: confounding and adjustment sets
atoms.essential_semantics: Which variables must be conditioned on for a causal estimand to be identified, derived from an assumed causal structure.
atoms.canonical_example: adjusting for Z blocks the backdoor path X <- Z -> Y
atoms.rationale: Adjustment validity is a graph-theoretic property of the assumed model, not a property of the data.

atoms.name: consistency
atoms.essential_semantics: Convergence of an estimator to the target as sample size grows, in a stated mode.
atoms.canonical_example: thetahat_n -> theta in probability
atoms.rationale: An asymptotic property that is meaningless without the mode of convergence and the sequence structure.

atoms.name: counterfactual quantities
atoms.essential_semantics: Potential outcomes Y(1), Y(0) for the same unit, only one of which is observed.
atoms.canonical_example: the individual treatment effect Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)
atoms.rationale: Counterfactuals are not expressible in the observational joint distribution alone; representing them requires extra structure.

atoms.name: credible interval
atoms.essential_semantics: An interval carrying posterior probability mass, a statement about the parameter given the data.
atoms.canonical_example: P(theta in [a,b] | x) = 0.95
atoms.rationale: Its interpretation differs fundamentally from a confidence interval; keeping them distinct is a real semantic requirement.

atoms.name: resampling-based evaluation
atoms.essential_semantics: A partitioning scheme respecting the dependence structure of the data, with the scheme itself part of the reported result.
atoms.canonical_example: 5-fold CV grouped by subject to avoid leakage
atoms.rationale: Leakage is a dependence-structure violation; representing the scheme makes it checkable.

atoms.name: dataset with declared structure
atoms.essential_semantics: An indexed collection of observations with unit of observation, variable names and per-variable measurement types.
atoms.canonical_example: n observations of (y_i, x_i) for i = 1..n
atoms.rationale: The unit of observation determines independence structure; an untyped table cannot express it.

atoms.name: design matrix and encoding of covariates
atoms.essential_semantics: Mapping from variables (including categorical ones) to columns, with the contrast/encoding scheme explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: a 3-level factor becomes 2 dummy columns under treatment coding
atoms.rationale: Coefficient interpretation depends entirely on the encoding, which is usually implicit and therefore lost.

atoms.name: effect size distinguished from significance
atoms.essential_semantics: A magnitude, typically with units or standardisation, separate from the evidence measure against a null.
atoms.canonical_example: a difference of 0.3 kg with p = 0.001
atoms.rationale: Magnitude and evidence are different quantities; conflating them is one of the field's standard failures.

atoms.name: efficiency, variance and MSE of an estimator
atoms.essential_semantics: Risk decomposition into bias and variance under a stated loss, and comparison against a bound.
atoms.canonical_example: MSE = bias^2 + variance; Cramer-Rao lower bound
atoms.rationale: Comparing estimators requires a loss function to be stated, not implied.

atoms.name: estimator as a function of data
atoms.essential_semantics: A rule mapping a dataset to a value, itself a random variable via the data; distinct from the estimate it produces.
atoms.canonical_example: the estimator Xbar_n versus the estimate 4.2
atoms.rationale: Sampling distributions are the pushforward of the data law under the estimator; without estimators as functions there is no sampling distribution.

atoms.name: Fisher information
atoms.essential_semantics: Expected negative Hessian of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter, a matrix-valued function of the parameter.
atoms.canonical_example: I(theta) = -E[d^2/dtheta^2 log L(theta; X)]
atoms.rationale: It composes differentiation, expectation and matrix structure in one object, a useful stress test.

atoms.name: generalised linear model with link and family
atoms.essential_semantics: A response family, a link function and a linear predictor as three separately identified components.
atoms.canonical_example: logit(E[Y|x]) = x^T beta with Y ~ Bernoulli
atoms.rationale: The link acts on the mean, not on the response; representations that apply it to the data are wrong.

atoms.name: null and alternative hypotheses
atoms.essential_semantics: Two disjoint subsets of the parameter space, with simple versus composite hypotheses distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: H0: mu = 0 versus H1: mu != 0
atoms.rationale: A hypothesis is a set of parameter values; representing it as a number makes composite hypotheses inexpressible.

atoms.name: identifiability of parameters
atoms.essential_semantics: Distinct parameter values induce distinct distributions; failure means the data cannot distinguish them.
atoms.canonical_example: in y = (a + b) x only a + b is identified
atoms.rationale: It is a quantified structural claim about a model, and an unidentified model produces confident nonsense.

atoms.name: likelihood as a function of the parameter
atoms.essential_semantics: The same formula as the density but with data fixed and parameter varying; a likelihood is not a probability distribution over parameters.
atoms.canonical_example: L(theta; x) = p(x | theta) viewed as a function of theta
atoms.rationale: The role reversal of arguments is the defining move of inference and is exactly the kind of fact a representation loses if it stores only a formula.

atoms.name: linear model with explicit error structure
atoms.essential_semantics: y = X beta + epsilon with the distribution of epsilon, the shape of X and the conditioning on X all stated.
atoms.canonical_example: y_i = beta_0 + beta_1 x_i + eps_i, eps_i iid Normal(0, sigma^2)
atoms.rationale: It is the most common applied model and simultaneously exercises shape typing, indexing and distributional assumptions.

atoms.name: log-likelihood and additivity over independent observations
atoms.essential_semantics: Sum over observations of log densities, valid only under an independence assumption that must be recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: l(theta) = sum_i log p(x_i | theta)
atoms.rationale: The additive form encodes an independence assumption; writing it without that assumption is a hidden modelling claim.

atoms.name: Markov chain Monte Carlo inference
atoms.essential_semantics: Approximating a posterior by a chain with a declared target, whose output is correlated samples, not exact draws.
atoms.canonical_example: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo targeting p(theta | x)
atoms.rationale: Convergence and autocorrelation qualifications are part of the inferential claim, not implementation trivia.

atoms.name: measurement scale of a variable
atoms.essential_semantics: Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scales determine which operations are meaningful (means of ordinals, ratios of interval data).
atoms.canonical_example: temperature in Celsius is interval, so ratios are meaningless
atoms.rationale: Stevens' scale typing is a genuine constraint on admissible operations that numeric typing alone does not capture.

atoms.name: missingness mechanism
atoms.essential_semantics: MCAR, MAR and MNAR as distinct conditional-independence assumptions about the missingness indicator.
atoms.canonical_example: missingness independent of the unobserved value given covariates (MAR)
atoms.rationale: The mechanism determines whether analysis is valid; it is an assumption that must be stated to be criticised.

atoms.name: random effects and grouped structure
atoms.essential_semantics: Parameters that are themselves random, indexed by group, with a covariance structure over groups.
atoms.canonical_example: y_ij = beta + u_j + eps_ij, u_j ~ Normal(0, tau^2)
atoms.rationale: Nested indexing plus random parameters is where flat modelling languages break down.

atoms.name: maximum likelihood estimation
atoms.essential_semantics: Argmax over a declared parameter space of the likelihood, with existence and uniqueness not assumed.
atoms.canonical_example: thetahat = argmax_{theta in Theta} L(theta; x)
atoms.rationale: It is the canonical composition of statistics with optimisation, including a constrained parameter space.

atoms.name: model comparison criteria
atoms.essential_semantics: Criteria such as AIC, BIC, WAIC with their assumptions and the comparability conditions (same data, same response scale).
atoms.canonical_example: AIC = -2 log L + 2k
atoms.rationale: Comparability preconditions are exactly the sort of side condition a faithful representation should carry.

atoms.name: multiplicity and error-rate control
atoms.essential_semantics: The number of tests performed and the family-wise or false-discovery criterion are part of the inferential claim.
atoms.canonical_example: Bonferroni adjustment across m tests
atoms.rationale: The family of tests is context that changes the meaning of each p-value; representing tests in isolation hides it.

atoms.name: observed versus latent quantity
atoms.essential_semantics: Which variables are observed and which are unobserved is part of the model, determining the likelihood and the inference target.
atoms.canonical_example: z_i latent class, y_i observed response
atoms.rationale: Latency drives marginalisation; a model that does not mark observability cannot derive its own likelihood.

atoms.name: population parameter versus sample statistic
atoms.essential_semantics: A population quantity (fixed, unknown) and a sample quantity (random, computed from data) are distinct objects with distinct types.
atoms.canonical_example: mu versus xbar
atoms.rationale: Every inferential error of the 'the mean is 5' kind stems from collapsing these; the distinction is the foundation of statistics.

atoms.name: posterior distribution
atoms.essential_semantics: The conditional distribution of parameters given data, distinct from the likelihood and from a point estimate.
atoms.canonical_example: p(theta | x)
atoms.rationale: The four-way distinction prior/likelihood/posterior/predictive is a hard test of distributional typing.

atoms.name: predictive distribution
atoms.essential_semantics: Distribution over new observations obtained by integrating the likelihood over the posterior.
atoms.canonical_example: p(xnew | x) = integral p(xnew | theta) p(theta | x) dtheta
atoms.rationale: It requires integrating a distribution-valued function over another distribution, a genuinely higher-order construction.

atoms.name: statistical power as a function of the alternative
atoms.essential_semantics: A function from the alternative parameter value to detection probability, not a single number.
atoms.canonical_example: power(delta) = P(reject H0 | mu = delta)
atoms.rationale: Reporting 'power = 0.8' without the effect size is an incomplete statement, which a typed representation would catch.

atoms.name: prior distribution over parameters
atoms.essential_semantics: A distribution over the parameter space, requiring parameters to be typed as random variables, with propriety declared.
atoms.canonical_example: theta ~ Beta(2, 2)
atoms.rationale: Treating a parameter as random is a substantive commitment; improper priors additionally require a propriety check on the posterior.

atoms.name: p-value
atoms.essential_semantics: Probability, under the null, of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed; a conditional probability of data given hypothesis, never of hypothesis given data.
atoms.canonical_example: p = P(T >= t_obs | H0)
atoms.rationale: The direction of conditioning is the most misinterpreted fact in applied statistics; a faithful representation must fix it.

atoms.name: residual versus error
atoms.essential_semantics: The unobservable error term and the computed residual are different objects with different distributions.
atoms.canonical_example: eps_i is unobserved; e_i = y_i - yhat_i is computed
atoms.rationale: Diagnostics rely on knowing that residuals are not the errors; the distinction is silently dropped in most notation.

atoms.name: sampling and experimental design
atoms.essential_semantics: How units were selected or assigned (randomisation, stratification, clustering, blocking), which determines valid inference.
atoms.canonical_example: stratified sample with unequal inclusion probabilities
atoms.rationale: Design is the bridge between data and population; analysis ignoring design is systematically biased.

atoms.name: sampling distribution of a statistic
atoms.essential_semantics: The law of an estimator under repeated sampling, dependent on the assumed data-generating process.
atoms.canonical_example: under normality, Xbar ~ Normal(mu, sigma^2/n)
atoms.rationale: Frequentist guarantees are statements about this distribution; if it cannot be named, the guarantees cannot be stated.

atoms.name: sufficient statistic
atoms.essential_semantics: A statistic carrying all information about a parameter, defined by conditional independence of the data from the parameter given the statistic.
atoms.canonical_example: sum of x_i is sufficient for the Poisson rate
atoms.rationale: A clean example of a statistical concept that is exactly a conditional-independence statement.

atoms.name: descriptive summaries with defined conventions
atoms.essential_semantics: Mean, median, quantiles, variance of a sample with denominator and interpolation conventions explicit and with population analogues distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: sample variance with denominator n-1
atoms.rationale: Convention differences (n versus n-1, quantile interpolation) change reported numbers and are almost never recorded.

atoms.name: test statistic and its null distribution
atoms.essential_semantics: A statistic together with its distribution under the null hypothesis, including whether that distribution is exact or asymptotic.
atoms.canonical_example: t = (xbar - mu0)/(s/sqrt(n)) ~ t_{n-1} under H0
atoms.rationale: The exact/asymptotic status of a null distribution is a validity condition that is routinely omitted.

atoms.name: time-indexed dependent data
atoms.essential_semantics: Observations with a temporal order and dependence, with stationarity assumptions explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: AR(1): y_t = phi y_{t-1} + eps_t
atoms.rationale: Independence-based inference fails here; the dependence assumption must be part of the model representation.

atoms.name: type I and type II error rates
atoms.essential_semantics: Error probabilities under the null and under a specified alternative respectively, both conditional and both procedure-level.
atoms.canonical_example: alpha = 0.05, beta depends on the true effect size
atoms.rationale: Type II error is defined only relative to an alternative, a dependency frequently left implicit.

atoms.name: variational approximation of a posterior
atoms.essential_semantics: Optimisation over a family of distributions minimising a divergence, with the family and divergence direction stated.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise KL(q || p) over mean-field Gaussian q
atoms.rationale: Optimising over distributions is optimisation whose decision variable is a measure, a demanding composition.

atoms.name: matrix representation of a graph
atoms.essential_semantics: A matrix view of a graph where the vertex ordering is an arbitrary choice and results should be order-invariant.
atoms.canonical_example: A_{ij} = 1 iff (i,j) in E
atoms.rationale: One object with two views (combinatorial and matrix) is a clean test of multi-representation support.

atoms.name: computational cost as a mathematical statement
atoms.essential_semantics: A cost function of input size with the machine model and the measured resource stated.
atoms.canonical_example: sorting requires Omega(n log n) comparisons
atoms.rationale: A cost claim without a model or resource is not falsifiable.

atoms.name: automaton / labelled transition system
atoms.essential_semantics: States, transitions and acceptance, with determinism declared.
atoms.canonical_example: a DFA accepting strings with an even number of a's
atoms.rationale: Included as the discrete-dynamics counterpart to Markov chains, marking a domain boundary.

atoms.name: binomial and multinomial coefficients
atoms.essential_semantics: Counting function with its domain conditions (0 <= k <= n or the convention of zero outside).
atoms.canonical_example: choose(5,2) = 10
atoms.rationale: It appears in every discrete distribution and its out-of-range convention affects computed probabilities.

atoms.name: Boolean algebra and normal forms
atoms.essential_semantics: Complemented distributive lattice with canonical normal forms (CNF, DNF) available.
atoms.canonical_example: conversion of a formula to conjunctive normal form
atoms.rationale: Normal forms are the canonicalisation story for propositional content.

atoms.name: partitions and colourings
atoms.essential_semantics: Assignments of labels subject to constraints, with the partition of a set as a derived object.
atoms.canonical_example: a proper 3-colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices
atoms.rationale: Constraint satisfaction over discrete labels, a standard hardness benchmark.

atoms.name: unordered selection
atoms.essential_semantics: Subsets of a given size, with and without repetition distinguished from ordered arrangements.
atoms.canonical_example: choose(n, k) subsets of size k
atoms.rationale: The ordered/unordered distinction is exactly what determines the correct count and hence the correct probability.

atoms.name: combinatorial identity with validity range
atoms.essential_semantics: Identities among counting expressions with the range of indices for which they hold.
atoms.canonical_example: sum_k choose(n,k) = 2^n for n >= 0
atoms.rationale: Universally quantified identities over a discrete domain, the natural target of induction.

atoms.name: complexity classes and reductions
atoms.essential_semantics: Classes of problems with reductions between them as the structuring relation.
atoms.canonical_example: 3-SAT is NP-complete
atoms.rationale: Included to mark the boundary between mathematical statements about problems and statements within them.

atoms.name: counting principles as reusable arguments
atoms.essential_semantics: Inclusion-exclusion, pigeonhole and bijective counting stated as principles with hypotheses.
atoms.canonical_example: if n items go into k < n boxes, some box has two items
atoms.rationale: Discrete existence proofs are counting arguments; representing the principle makes the reasoning explicit.

atoms.name: directed acyclic graph with acyclicity as a checked property
atoms.essential_semantics: A directed graph with no directed cycles, where acyclicity is verified rather than assumed.
atoms.canonical_example: a Bayesian network structure
atoms.rationale: Generative models and causal graphs must be acyclic to define a joint distribution; a cycle silently invalidates the model.

atoms.name: directed graph
atoms.essential_semantics: Edges as ordered pairs, with in/out degree and direction preserved by all operations.
atoms.canonical_example: an edge from u to v does not imply one from v to u
atoms.rationale: Causal and dependency structures are directed; losing direction is a total loss of the causal claim.

atoms.name: factorial and falling/rising powers
atoms.essential_semantics: Standard combinatorial functions on naturals with their conventions (0! = 1) fixed.
atoms.canonical_example: n! = product from 1 to n, with 0! = 1
atoms.rationale: Small, but a canonical instance where a boundary convention must be pinned rather than assumed.

atoms.name: network flow with conservation constraints
atoms.essential_semantics: Edge-indexed variables with per-vertex conservation and capacity constraints.
atoms.canonical_example: max flow subject to conservation at every internal node
atoms.rationale: Indexed constraint families over a graph structure exercise scoped constraint generation.

atoms.name: formal language and grammar
atoms.essential_semantics: Sets of strings defined by a grammar, with ambiguity of the grammar itself a meaningful property.
atoms.canonical_example: a context-free grammar and whether it is ambiguous
atoms.rationale: Relevant to any system that must reason about its own or another notation's grammar.

atoms.name: generating function
atoms.essential_semantics: A formal power series encoding a sequence, where formal manipulation is distinguished from analytic convergence.
atoms.canonical_example: sum a_n x^n as a formal series
atoms.rationale: The formal/analytic distinction is a real one that a representation should not collapse.

atoms.name: graph as vertices plus edges
atoms.essential_semantics: A vertex set with an edge relation, with simplicity, loops and multi-edges declared.
atoms.canonical_example: G = (V, E) with E a set of unordered pairs
atoms.rationale: Graph structure is a mathematical object with variants that change every theorem about it.

atoms.name: indexed maximum, minimum and argmax over a finite set
atoms.essential_semantics: Extremum over an index set with ties and emptiness handled explicitly.
atoms.canonical_example: argmax_{i in I} score_i, undefined for empty I
atoms.rationale: Ties and empty ranges are real cases that a representation must be able to state rather than silently resolve.

atoms.name: lattice with meet and join
atoms.essential_semantics: A partial order with binary greatest lower and least upper bounds, used for type joins and abstract domains.
atoms.canonical_example: the meet of Probability and PositiveReal is NonNegativeReal
atoms.rationale: Type unification and static analysis are lattice computations; without meets, incomparable types cannot be combined principledly.

atoms.name: matchings, covers and independent sets
atoms.essential_semantics: Combinatorial substructures defined by constraints, whose optimisation versions are standard problems.
atoms.canonical_example: a maximum matching in a bipartite graph
atoms.rationale: Canonical combinatorial optimisation objects requiring constraint expression over discrete structures.

atoms.name: multiset with multiplicities
atoms.essential_semantics: A collection where repetition counts but order does not, distinct from both a set and a sequence.
atoms.canonical_example: the multiset of observed values {1, 1, 2}
atoms.rationale: Data samples are multisets; representing them as sets loses duplicates and as sequences imposes spurious order.

atoms.name: partial order and incomparability
atoms.essential_semantics: A reflexive antisymmetric transitive relation in which two elements may be incomparable, distinct from a total order.
atoms.canonical_example: subset inclusion is a partial order; {1} and {2} are incomparable
atoms.rationale: Incomparability is a positive fact, not missing information; Pareto dominance and type lattices depend on it.

atoms.name: paths, reachability and connectivity
atoms.essential_semantics: Walks, paths and cycles distinguished; reachability as a relation derived from the edge relation.
atoms.canonical_example: there is a directed path from X to Y
atoms.rationale: Backdoor criteria and dependency analysis are path statements.

atoms.name: permutation and arrangement
atoms.essential_semantics: A bijection of a finite set onto itself or an ordered selection, with composition and inverse available.
atoms.canonical_example: the number of permutations of n objects is n!
atoms.rationale: Symmetry arguments and exchangeability are permutation statements.

atoms.name: indexed product
atoms.essential_semantics: Binds an index and multiplies, with the empty-product convention and non-commutative cases handled by preserving order.
atoms.canonical_example: product_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i), empty product equal to 1
atoms.rationale: Likelihoods are indexed products; ordering matters when the factors are matrices.

atoms.name: recurrence relation with initial conditions
atoms.essential_semantics: A defining relation over an index with the required number of initial values, distinct from a closed form.
atoms.rationale: Recurrences with insufficient initial conditions do not define a sequence; the count is a checkable condition.

atoms.name: sequence indexed by naturals
atoms.essential_semantics: An ordered, possibly infinite family with a defined index origin and a rule or listing.
atoms.canonical_example: a_n = 1/n for n >= 1
atoms.rationale: Sequences underlie limits, series and iterative algorithms; index-origin conventions are a genuine source of error.

atoms.name: finite set with cardinality
atoms.essential_semantics: An extensionally or intensionally given finite collection whose size is available and whose elements are unordered and distinct.
atoms.rationale: Finite sample spaces, index sets and vocabularies are finite sets; unorderedness and distinctness are semantic, not incidental.

atoms.name: summation with an explicit index and range
atoms.essential_semantics: Binds an index over a stated range or index set, including empty-range conventions and multi-index sums.
atoms.canonical_example: sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i, with the empty sum equal to 0
atoms.rationale: Summation is the most frequent binder in applied mathematics after quantifiers; the index set is semantic content, not syntax.

atoms.name: tree and rooted hierarchy
atoms.essential_semantics: Acyclic connected graph, possibly rooted with parent/child structure.
atoms.canonical_example: a decision tree or a nested grouping structure
atoms.rationale: Nested experimental designs and hierarchical indices are trees.

atoms.name: weighted and labelled graphs
atoms.essential_semantics: Edge or vertex attributes with their own types and possibly units.
atoms.canonical_example: edge weights in kilometres
atoms.rationale: Network optimisation attaches typed quantities to edges; untyped weights admit unit errors.

atoms.name: affine space and affine combinations
atoms.essential_semantics: A space acted on freely and transitively by a vector space, where only weight-one combinations of points are defined.
atoms.canonical_example: the midpoint (P + Q)/2 is affine; P + Q is not
atoms.rationale: Convex combinations are affine combinations with non-negative weights; the affine structure is what makes them legitimate.

atoms.name: angle with units and range convention
atoms.essential_semantics: Angles as dimensionless-but-unit-bearing quantities with radian/degree distinguished and the principal range stated.
atoms.canonical_example: atan2 returns an angle in (-pi, pi]
atoms.rationale: Degree/radian confusion is a classic real-world failure, and angle is the canonical dimensionless-with-unit case.

atoms.name: charts, atlases and coordinate patches
atoms.essential_semantics: Local coordinates valid on a patch, with transition maps on overlaps; no global coordinates assumed.
atoms.canonical_example: latitude-longitude fails at the poles
atoms.rationale: Local-only validity is a general and underappreciated pattern that a representation should be able to record.

atoms.name: compactness
atoms.essential_semantics: Every open cover has a finite subcover, with the Heine-Borel characterisation valid only in specific settings.
atoms.canonical_example: a continuous function on a compact set attains its maximum
atoms.rationale: Existence of extrema is a compactness theorem; asserting attainment without it is unjustified.

atoms.name: cones and generalised inequalities
atoms.essential_semantics: A closed convex cone inducing a partial order, such as the PSD cone with the Loewner order.
atoms.canonical_example: A preceq B means B - A is positive semidefinite
atoms.rationale: Matrix inequalities are cone inequalities, not elementwise ones; conflating them is a real modelling error.

atoms.name: connectedness and path-connectedness
atoms.essential_semantics: Distinct notions with an implication in only one direction, both relative to a topology.
atoms.canonical_example: the intermediate value theorem needs connectedness of the domain
atoms.rationale: Domain connectivity is a hypothesis in several standard theorems and is often assumed silently for piecewise domains.

atoms.name: continuous map between spaces
atoms.essential_semantics: Preimages of open sets are open; continuity is relative to the topologies on both source and target.
atoms.canonical_example: f : (X, tau_X) -> (Y, tau_Y) continuous
atoms.rationale: It generalises analytic continuity and parallels measurability, both of which are two-structure relations.

atoms.name: convex set
atoms.essential_semantics: Closed under convex combinations, with convexity as a checkable property of a described set.
atoms.canonical_example: {x : Ax <= b} is convex
atoms.rationale: Convexity of the feasible set is the property that makes optimisation tractable and local optima global.

atoms.name: change of coordinates with Jacobian factor
atoms.essential_semantics: Transformation between coordinate systems including the volume-element correction.
atoms.canonical_example: dA = r dr dtheta in polar coordinates
atoms.rationale: Forgetting the Jacobian factor is a canonical silent error shared by geometry and probability.

atoms.name: named coordinate system
atoms.essential_semantics: Cartesian, polar, spherical, cylindrical with the convention (angle order, sign) explicit and the validity region stated.
atoms.canonical_example: (r, theta) with r >= 0 and theta in [0, 2 pi)
atoms.rationale: Coordinate conventions differ between fields and change integration measures; leaving them implicit is lossy.

atoms.name: curvature
atoms.essential_semantics: Local deviation from flatness, derived from the metric, with the specific curvature notion identified.
atoms.canonical_example: Gaussian curvature of a sphere is 1/r^2
atoms.rationale: Included to bound the geometric end of the ontology; low expectation for a general mathematical IR.

atoms.name: differential forms and orientation
atoms.essential_semantics: Antisymmetric multilinear objects integrated over oriented submanifolds, with exterior derivative.
atoms.canonical_example: Stokes theorem: integral of d omega over M equals integral of omega over the boundary
atoms.rationale: It is the correct type of an integrand on a manifold, distinct from a scalar function.

atoms.name: distance with an identified metric
atoms.essential_semantics: Which metric is being used (Euclidean, Manhattan, geodesic, Mahalanobis) is part of the statement.
atoms.canonical_example: Mahalanobis distance uses Sigma^{-1}
atoms.rationale: Unqualified 'distance' is ambiguous and the choice changes results; it also carries units.

atoms.name: Euclidean space with dimension
atoms.essential_semantics: R^n with the standard inner product, where the dimension is part of the type.
atoms.canonical_example: x in R^3
atoms.rationale: The default ambient space for applied geometry and multivariate analysis; dimension mismatch is a checkable error.

atoms.name: geodesic and shortest path
atoms.essential_semantics: Locally length-minimising curve determined by the metric, whose existence and uniqueness are conditional.
atoms.canonical_example: great circles on a sphere
atoms.rationale: A variational problem on a manifold, combining several capabilities at once.

atoms.name: homeomorphism and topological invariants
atoms.essential_semantics: Bicontinuous bijection; invariants are properties preserved by it.
atoms.canonical_example: a circle and a square are homeomorphic
atoms.rationale: The topological analogue of isomorphism, useful for testing whether structural equivalence is representable.

atoms.name: homotopy and deformation
atoms.essential_semantics: Continuous deformation between maps, generating invariants such as the fundamental group.
atoms.canonical_example: a loop in the punctured plane has a winding number
atoms.rationale: Included to mark the far end of topological expressiveness rather than as an expected capability.

atoms.name: manifold with dimension and smoothness
atoms.essential_semantics: A space locally homeomorphic to R^n with a declared dimension and smoothness class.
atoms.canonical_example: the sphere S^2 as a 2-dimensional smooth manifold
atoms.rationale: Constraint surfaces and parameter spaces with structure (simplex, positive-definite cone) are manifolds.

atoms.name: volume, area and surface measures
atoms.essential_semantics: Measures induced by the geometry, with dimension-dependent units and the correct measure for a submanifold.
atoms.canonical_example: surface area measure on the sphere
atoms.rationale: Uniform distributions on geometric domains require the right base measure; getting it wrong changes the distribution.

atoms.name: metric tensor and induced geometry
atoms.essential_semantics: A field of inner products determining lengths, angles and volumes, possibly non-Euclidean.
atoms.canonical_example: the Fisher information metric on a statistical manifold
atoms.rationale: Information geometry and relativity both need a non-flat metric; assuming Euclidean geometry is a modelling commitment.

atoms.name: open, closed, interior, closure, boundary
atoms.essential_semantics: These are properties relative to an ambient space, and open and closed are not complementary properties of sets.
atoms.canonical_example: [0,1) is neither open nor closed in R
atoms.rationale: Whether a feasible set is closed determines whether an optimum is attained; a real practical consequence.

atoms.name: orientation and handedness
atoms.essential_semantics: A choice of sign convention for ordered bases or boundaries, preserved through transformations.
atoms.canonical_example: a right-handed coordinate frame
atoms.rationale: Sign conventions in physics and graphics are orientation choices that must survive translation between systems.

atoms.name: point versus displacement vector
atoms.essential_semantics: Points and vectors are different types: point minus point is a vector, point plus vector is a point, point plus point is meaningless.
atoms.canonical_example: P - Q is a displacement; P + Q is not defined
atoms.rationale: The affine/linear distinction is the geometric analogue of the interval/ratio scale distinction and prevents a real class of errors.

atoms.name: polyhedra and polytopes
atoms.essential_semantics: Intersections of half-spaces with vertex and facet descriptions as alternative views of one object.
atoms.canonical_example: the feasible region of a linear program
atoms.rationale: H-representation and V-representation are two faithful views of one object, a good multi-view test.

atoms.name: projection onto a set or subspace
atoms.essential_semantics: Nearest-point map relative to a metric, with existence and uniqueness requiring convexity and closedness.
atoms.canonical_example: least-squares fit projects y onto the column space of X
atoms.rationale: Least squares is a projection statement; the geometric view carries the orthogonality condition explicitly.

atoms.name: probability simplex as a constrained domain
atoms.essential_semantics: Non-negative vectors summing to one, a constrained manifold that is not an open subset of R^n.
atoms.canonical_example: p in Delta^{k-1}: p_i >= 0, sum p_i = 1
atoms.rationale: Categorical parameters live on the simplex; treating them as free vectors produces invalid gradients and invalid samples.

atoms.name: tangent space at a point
atoms.essential_semantics: A vector space attached to each point, where the base point is part of the vector's identity.
atoms.canonical_example: v in T_p M
atoms.rationale: Gradients on constrained spaces live in tangent spaces; ignoring the base point produces invalid updates.

atoms.name: topological space
atoms.essential_semantics: A set with a declared topology, so that continuity and convergence are relative to a named structure.
atoms.canonical_example: (X, tau) with tau a collection of open sets
atoms.rationale: Topology is the minimal structure for continuity; assuming the standard topology on R^n is an unrecorded commitment.

atoms.name: group of transformations and invariance
atoms.essential_semantics: Rotations, translations, similarities acting on a space, with invariance of a quantity as a statable property.
atoms.canonical_example: the Euclidean distance is invariant under rigid motions
atoms.rationale: Invariance claims are a major class of mathematical statement and require the group to be nameable.

atoms.name: vector field
atoms.essential_semantics: An assignment of a tangent vector to each point, with divergence and curl as derived operations.
atoms.canonical_example: the velocity field of a fluid
atoms.rationale: Physical fields are point-indexed vectors with units; representing them as arrays loses both.

atoms.name: argmin/argmax as a set-valued binder
atoms.essential_semantics: The set of optimisers, which may be empty or non-singleton, distinguished from the optimal value.
atoms.canonical_example: argmin_{x in C} f(x) may contain several points
atoms.rationale: Returning a single point as 'the' argmin asserts uniqueness that is often unproven and sometimes false.

atoms.name: Bellman equation / recursive optimality
atoms.essential_semantics: A fixed-point equation over value functions combining optimisation and expectation.
atoms.canonical_example: V(s) = max_a [ r(s,a) + gamma E_{s'}[V(s')] ]
atoms.rationale: It nests a max inside an expectation inside a recursion, a demanding composition of three capabilities.

atoms.name: variable bounds and domain restrictions
atoms.essential_semantics: Simple per-variable bounds recognised as constraints on the decision domain, possibly with units.
atoms.canonical_example: 0 <= x_i <= 1 for all i
atoms.rationale: Bounds indexed over a family are the most common constraint pattern and require quantified constraint generation.

atoms.name: probabilistic (chance) constraint
atoms.essential_semantics: A constraint required to hold with at least a given probability, mixing a quantifier over outcomes with a probability threshold.
atoms.rationale: It is the clearest case where a constraint is not a deterministic proposition but a probabilistic one.

atoms.name: conic and semidefinite programs
atoms.essential_semantics: Constraints expressed as membership in a cone, including matrix inequalities in the PSD cone.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise tr(CX) subject to X positive semidefinite
atoms.rationale: Matrix-valued decision variables with cone constraints stress shape typing and generalised inequalities together.

atoms.name: scoped and conditional constraints
atoms.essential_semantics: A constraint that applies only within a scope, over an index subset, or under a stated condition, without leaking globally.
atoms.canonical_example: for all i in ActiveSet, x_i <= c_i
atoms.rationale: Constraint scope is a binding phenomenon; systems with a global constraint store cannot represent locally-valid constraints correctly.

atoms.name: convexity of objective and constraints
atoms.essential_semantics: Convexity as a checkable property, with the convex-problem form (convex objective, convex feasible set) recognised.
atoms.canonical_example: a convex program has every local minimum global
atoms.rationale: Convexity determines which guarantees apply; asserting global optimality without it is unjustified.

atoms.name: decision variable with a declared domain
atoms.essential_semantics: A symbol optimised over, distinguished from data, parameters and constants, with an explicit domain.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise over x in R^n
atoms.rationale: An optimisation problem is defined by which symbols are free to vary; if data and decision variables are not distinguished the problem is not specified.

atoms.name: minimisation versus maximisation
atoms.essential_semantics: The optimisation sense is explicit and is not recoverable from the objective alone.
atoms.canonical_example: maximise log-likelihood equals minimise negative log-likelihood
atoms.rationale: A sign error here inverts the answer; the sense must be part of the representation, not a convention of the solver.

atoms.name: dual problem and duality gap
atoms.essential_semantics: A derived problem whose value bounds the primal, with weak duality always and strong duality conditional.
atoms.canonical_example: strong duality holds for convex problems under Slater's condition
atoms.rationale: The conditionality of strong duality is a classic side condition that must not be assumed.

atoms.name: sequential decision problems
atoms.essential_semantics: Decisions over stages with a state, transition and stagewise cost, exploiting the Markov structure.
atoms.canonical_example: finite-horizon dynamic program with value iteration
atoms.rationale: Stagewise structure is a modelling assumption with strong consequences and should be explicit.

atoms.name: equality constraint
atoms.essential_semantics: A constraint of the form h(x) = 0 that is part of the problem, distinct from a definition or an assignment.
atoms.canonical_example: subject to sum_i p_i = 1
atoms.rationale: Constraints are propositions attached to a problem; conflating them with definitions destroys the problem structure.

atoms.name: objective containing an expectation
atoms.essential_semantics: Optimising E[f(x, X)] where the expectation is over a distribution that may itself depend on x, with the dependence explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise E_{X ~ p}[loss(x, X)]
atoms.rationale: Whether the distribution depends on the decision variable determines whether the gradient can be moved inside the expectation; that dependence must be representable.

atoms.name: feasible set
atoms.essential_semantics: The set of admissible decisions defined by the constraints, which may be empty, and whose emptiness is a meaningful result.
atoms.rationale: Infeasibility is a legitimate outcome; a representation that cannot express an empty feasible set will report a wrong answer instead.

atoms.name: derivative of an objective with respect to decisions
atoms.essential_semantics: Gradient taken with respect to the decision variables only, holding data and parameters fixed, with shape matching the decision domain.
atoms.canonical_example: grad_x f(x; theta), not grad_theta
atoms.rationale: Which variable the derivative is taken with respect to is the essential fact, and it is exactly what is lost when derivatives are written without their variable.

atoms.name: inequality constraint
atoms.essential_semantics: Constraint g(x) <= 0 with strictness recorded and with active/inactive status meaningful at a solution.
atoms.canonical_example: subject to x >= 0
atoms.rationale: Active-set reasoning and KKT conditions require inequality constraints as distinct objects with a strictness flag.

atoms.name: integrality and discrete decisions
atoms.essential_semantics: Decision variables restricted to integers or a finite set, a domain restriction rather than a constraint on a real variable.
atoms.canonical_example: x in {0, 1}^n
atoms.rationale: Relaxing integrality changes the problem; the distinction must be visible in the representation.

atoms.name: first-order optimality conditions
atoms.essential_semantics: Stationarity, primal and dual feasibility and complementary slackness, valid under constraint qualifications.
atoms.canonical_example: lambda_i g_i(x) = 0 for all i
atoms.rationale: KKT is necessary only under qualifications; stating it unconditionally is a false theorem.

atoms.name: Lagrangian and multipliers
atoms.essential_semantics: Objective plus multiplier-weighted constraints, with multipliers as typed objects carrying units of objective per constraint.
atoms.canonical_example: L(x, lambda) = f(x) + lambda^T g(x)
atoms.rationale: Multipliers are shadow prices with derived units; a representation that keeps units must handle them.

atoms.name: linear program
atoms.essential_semantics: Linear objective and linear constraints recognised as a problem class, with linearity checkable rather than asserted.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise c^T x subject to Ax <= b, x >= 0
atoms.rationale: Problem-class recognition determines which solvers and guarantees apply; it should follow from the structure, not a user label.

atoms.name: local versus global optimality
atoms.essential_semantics: The scope of an optimality claim is explicit, with the neighbourhood identified for local claims.
atoms.canonical_example: a local minimum of a non-convex objective need not be global
atoms.rationale: Reporting a local optimum as the solution is a substantive overstatement that a faithful representation prevents.

atoms.name: mixed continuous-discrete problems
atoms.essential_semantics: Problems with both variable kinds, with logical constraints (implications, disjunctions) among them.
atoms.canonical_example: if y = 1 then x <= M, encoded as a big-M constraint
atoms.rationale: Logical structure inside constraints is where modelling languages either express implications directly or force error-prone encodings.

atoms.name: multiple objectives and Pareto optimality
atoms.essential_semantics: Several objectives with a partial order on outcomes, where the solution is a frontier rather than a point.
atoms.canonical_example: the Pareto frontier trading cost against risk
atoms.rationale: Scalarising multiple objectives without saying so imposes a weighting that is a hidden modelling decision.

atoms.name: objective function
atoms.essential_semantics: A scalar-valued function of the decision variables, possibly depending on data and parameters, identified as the quantity being optimised.
atoms.rationale: Optimisation is a pervasive mathematical activity and the objective must be a nameable object to be differentiated, bounded, or compared.

atoms.name: optimal control over a dynamical system
atoms.essential_semantics: Optimisation of a functional subject to dynamics as constraints, with state and control distinguished.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise integral of cost subject to xdot = f(x, u)
atoms.rationale: Constraints that are differential equations require constraint objects capable of holding functional relations.

atoms.name: optimal value versus optimiser
atoms.essential_semantics: The extremal value of the objective, possibly an infimum not attained, distinct from the point achieving it and possibly infinite.
atoms.canonical_example: inf_{x > 0} x = 0 but is not attained
atoms.rationale: Attainment requires hypotheses (compactness, closedness, coercivity) that must be stated rather than presumed.

atoms.name: optimisation as a function of parameters
atoms.essential_semantics: The optimal value and optimiser as functions of problem data, supporting sensitivity analysis.
atoms.canonical_example: v(b) = min {c^T x : Ax <= b}
atoms.rationale: Differentiating through an optimisation problem requires the value function to be an object, not a number.

atoms.name: optimisation problem as a first-class object
atoms.essential_semantics: The whole problem (variables, objective, constraints, sense) is one nameable object that can be transformed, relaxed or compared.
atoms.canonical_example: P' is the LP relaxation of P
atoms.rationale: Reformulation, relaxation and dualisation are transformations on problems; without the problem as an object they cannot be expressed.

atoms.name: quadratic program
atoms.essential_semantics: Quadratic objective with the definiteness of the quadratic form determining convexity.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise (1/2) x^T Q x + c^T x with Q positive semidefinite
atoms.rationale: Least squares and regularised regression are QPs whose tractability depends on a matrix property.

atoms.name: regularisation and penalty terms
atoms.essential_semantics: Additional objective terms with a weight whose units must be compatible with the loss, and with the norm identified.
atoms.canonical_example: minimise ||Ax - b||^2 + lambda ||x||_1
atoms.rationale: Adding terms with different units is a dimensional error that a unit-aware representation catches; the choice of norm is also semantic.

atoms.name: robust / minimax formulation
atoms.essential_semantics: Optimising against the worst case over an uncertainty set, an inherently alternating-quantifier structure.
atoms.canonical_example: min_x max_{u in U} f(x, u)
atoms.rationale: min-max and max-min differ; this is quantifier order appearing directly in an optimisation problem.

atoms.name: optimisation over functions or distributions
atoms.essential_semantics: The decision variable is a function or a measure, with the admissible class stated.
atoms.canonical_example: min over distributions q in Q of KL(q || p)
atoms.rationale: Infinite-dimensional decision variables are common in modern statistics and require function-typed optimisation.

atoms.name: affine (offset) units and the difference/absolute distinction
atoms.essential_semantics: Units with a non-zero origin (Celsius, Fahrenheit, dates) where differences are ratio-scaled but absolutes are not, so multiplication by a scalar is invalid.
atoms.canonical_example: a 10 degC rise is 10 K, but 10 degC is 283.15 K
atoms.rationale: Doubling a temperature in Celsius is meaningless; this is the unit-level analogue of the point/vector distinction and is very commonly wrong.

atoms.name: declared system of base dimensions
atoms.essential_semantics: The set of independent base dimensions is declared (SI's seven, or a domain-specific set) and extensible, rather than hard-coded.
atoms.canonical_example: SI base dimensions: L, M, T, I, Theta, N, J
atoms.rationale: Different fields use different base sets (e.g. adding currency or information); a fixed set silently excludes those domains.

atoms.name: conservation and balance relations
atoms.essential_semantics: A statement that a quantity's total is invariant or that inflow equals outflow, checkable dimensionally and structurally.
atoms.canonical_example: mass in equals mass out plus accumulation
atoms.rationale: Balance equations are a recurring scientific pattern whose dimensional consistency is a strong correctness signal.

atoms.name: reference frame of a physical quantity
atoms.essential_semantics: Vector quantities are expressed relative to a named frame, and combining quantities from different frames requires an explicit transformation.
atoms.canonical_example: velocity expressed in the body frame versus the inertial frame
atoms.rationale: Frame mismatch is the vector analogue of unit mismatch and causes equally serious errors in engineering.

atoms.name: counts, proportions and rates distinguished
atoms.essential_semantics: A dimensionless count, a proportion in [0,1] and a rate per unit of something are different quantity kinds despite all being numbers.
atoms.canonical_example: 17 events, 0.34 proportion, 2.1 events per hour
atoms.rationale: Poisson rates versus counts versus proportions are routinely mixed up in modelling, and the confusion is representable and preventable.

atoms.name: physical dimension as a type-level attribute
atoms.essential_semantics: A quantity carries a dimension (length, mass, time, ...) expressible as a vector of exponents over base dimensions, checked independently of the chosen unit.
atoms.canonical_example: velocity has dimension L T^-1
atoms.rationale: Dimensional analysis is a checkable soundness discipline over scientific mathematics; dimension is coarser and more robust than unit and must be tracked separately.

atoms.name: dimensional homogeneity checking
atoms.essential_semantics: Addition, subtraction, comparison and equality require matching dimensions; violation is rejected rather than coerced.
atoms.canonical_example: 1 m + 1 s is rejected
atoms.rationale: This is the primary payoff of unit tracking; a system that tracks units but does not enforce homogeneity gains nothing semantically.

atoms.name: dimensionless quantities
atoms.essential_semantics: Quantities whose dimension vector is zero, which may still carry a unit-like tag (radian, percent, dB) that is semantically meaningful.
atoms.canonical_example: a strain of 0.002, an angle in radians
atoms.rationale: Dimensionless is not the same as unitless; radians and percent are dimensionless but not interchangeable.

atoms.name: dimensionless groups and the Buckingham pi theorem
atoms.essential_semantics: Named combinations that are dimensionless by construction, with derivation from the dimension matrix.
atoms.canonical_example: Reynolds number Re = rho v L / mu
atoms.rationale: It shows dimensional analysis has real inferential content (a rank computation), not merely a checking role.

atoms.name: logarithmic scales and reference values
atoms.essential_semantics: Log-scaled quantities (dB, pH, magnitudes) are logs of ratios to a stated reference, and the reference is part of the quantity.
atoms.canonical_example: dB SPL is referenced to 20 micropascals
atoms.rationale: Reporting decibels without a reference is an incomplete quantity, a small but real semantic omission.

atoms.name: physical constants with units and provenance
atoms.essential_semantics: Named constants carrying a unit, an uncertainty and a defining source, with exact-by-definition constants distinguished from measured ones.
atoms.canonical_example: c = 299792458 m/s exactly; G is measured with uncertainty
atoms.rationale: The exact/measured distinction among constants directly affects error propagation.

atoms.name: metric prefixes and scale factors
atoms.essential_semantics: Prefixes as exact powers of ten (or two) composed with a base unit, not as separate units.
atoms.canonical_example: 1 km = 10^3 m exactly
atoms.rationale: Prefix handling determines whether km and m canonicalise together; getting it wrong produces spurious incompatibilities.

atoms.name: quantity as value plus unit
atoms.essential_semantics: A single object pairing a magnitude with a unit, where the numeric magnitude alone is not the quantity.
atoms.rationale: Quantities compose with almost everything else in the ontology; if the unit is not attached to the value it will be lost at the first operation.

atoms.name: precision of a reported value
atoms.essential_semantics: The number of meaningful digits is information about the value and is not increased by arithmetic.
atoms.canonical_example: 2.0 m is not the same claim as 2.000 m
atoms.rationale: Reporting more digits than justified is a common way computation manufactures false confidence.

atoms.name: units on vector, matrix and tensor components
atoms.essential_semantics: A unit may apply uniformly to a tensor or vary per component (as in a mixed-unit state vector), and this must be representable.
atoms.canonical_example: a state vector holding position in m and velocity in m/s
atoms.rationale: Mixed-unit vectors are common in control and state-space models and break naive per-array unit tagging.

atoms.name: instants versus durations
atoms.essential_semantics: A time instant is a point on an affine timeline and a duration is a vector; only durations may be added or scaled.
atoms.canonical_example: t2 - t1 is a duration; t1 + t2 is meaningless
atoms.rationale: Time-series modelling constantly mixes instants and durations; it is the most frequently encountered affine-unit case.

atoms.name: measurement uncertainty attached to a quantity
atoms.essential_semantics: A value with a stated uncertainty and its interpretation (standard uncertainty, coverage interval), distinct from a probability distribution but relatable to one.
atoms.rationale: Uncertainty is a first-class attribute of measured data; dropping it converts a measurement into a false exact value.

atoms.name: propagation of uncertainty through operations
atoms.essential_semantics: Derived quantities carry uncertainties computed under stated assumptions (linearisation, independence of inputs).
atoms.canonical_example: for z = xy, relative uncertainties add in quadrature if x and y are independent
atoms.rationale: The independence assumption behind quadrature addition is usually unstated and often false.

atoms.name: unit of measurement
atoms.essential_semantics: A named scale for a dimension, where two units of the same dimension are convertible and units of different dimensions are not.
atoms.canonical_example: metre, foot and mile all have dimension L
atoms.rationale: Unit-mismatch failures are documented, expensive and entirely preventable by representation.

atoms.name: random variables and distribution parameters with units
atoms.essential_semantics: A random variable may be dimensionful, in which case location and scale parameters share its unit, variance has squared units, and shape parameters must be dimensionless.
atoms.canonical_example: H ~ Normal(mu = 1.7 m, sigma = 0.1 m), Var(H) in m^2
atoms.rationale: The interaction of units with distribution parameter roles is a demanding cross-domain composition that almost no system handles fully.

atoms.name: algebra of compound units
atoms.essential_semantics: Units multiply, divide and take rational powers, with a canonical form so that equivalent compound units compare equal.
atoms.canonical_example: N = kg m s^-2; J/s = W
atoms.rationale: Without canonicalisation of compound units, dimensionally equal quantities are wrongly reported as incompatible or vice versa.

atoms.name: conversion between commensurable units
atoms.essential_semantics: Exact or documented conversion factors between units of the same dimension, with the conversion recorded as a transformation rather than silently applied.
atoms.canonical_example: 1 inch = 25.4 mm exactly
atoms.rationale: Some conversions are exact and some are approximate; conflating them injects unrecorded error.

atoms.name: dimensionless-argument requirement for transcendental functions
atoms.essential_semantics: exp, log, sin and similar require dimensionless arguments; a dimensionful argument must be rejected or explained.
atoms.canonical_example: log(x) with x in metres is ill-formed; log(x/x0) is not
atoms.rationale: It is a sharp, mechanically checkable rule that catches a whole class of modelling errors, notably in log-transformed regressions.

atoms.name: units of a derivative
atoms.essential_semantics: d y / d x has the unit of y divided by the unit of x, computed automatically and correctly for higher orders.
atoms.canonical_example: d(position in m)/d(time in s) is m/s; the second derivative is m/s^2
atoms.rationale: A unit system that does not derive derivative units is not integrated with the calculus and will silently drop or corrupt units.

atoms.name: units of an integral
atoms.essential_semantics: The differential contributes its unit: integrating y d x yields units of y times units of x.
atoms.canonical_example: integral of power (W) dt (s) yields energy (J)
atoms.rationale: The measure carries units; this is also why a probability density has reciprocal units of its variate, a fact almost always lost.

atoms.name: absolute error
atoms.essential_semantics: The difference between a computed and an exact quantity, carrying the same units as the quantity.
atoms.canonical_example: |xhat - x| <= 1e-6 metres
atoms.rationale: Error claims are meaningless unless absolute and relative are distinguished and units are carried.

atoms.name: approximation as a first-class relation
atoms.essential_semantics: 'approximately equal' is a distinct relation from equality, carrying an error magnitude or bound, and is not transitive without accounting.
atoms.canonical_example: pi ≈ 3.1416 with error below 1e-4
atoms.rationale: Writing '=' where only '≈' holds is the most common way a computational representation overstates what it knows, and chained approximations accumulate error that must be tracked.

atoms.name: algorithmic differentiation
atoms.essential_semantics: Exact-to-rounding derivatives of a program, distinguished from symbolic differentiation and from finite differences, with mode (forward/reverse) and differentiability preconditions.
atoms.canonical_example: reverse-mode gradient of a scalar loss over n parameters
atoms.rationale: AD silently returns a one-sided value at non-differentiable points; this is a real correctness gap worth representing.

atoms.name: cost of evaluating a mathematical object
atoms.essential_semantics: The computational cost of evaluating an expression, distinguished from the mathematical content of the expression itself.
atoms.canonical_example: the determinant is defined combinatorially but computed by factorisation
atoms.rationale: Keeping definition and evaluation strategy separate is what allows one statement to have several implementations.

atoms.name: conditioning of a problem
atoms.essential_semantics: Sensitivity of the output to input perturbation, a property of the problem independent of the algorithm.
atoms.rationale: Ill-conditioning explains why a correct algorithm gives a wrong-looking answer; separating it from stability is essential.

atoms.name: rate and order of convergence
atoms.essential_semantics: How fast an iterative or discretised method approaches its limit, with the order and the asymptotic regime stated.
atoms.canonical_example: Newton's method converges quadratically near a simple root
atoms.rationale: Rates hold only locally or under hypotheses; unqualified rate claims are frequently false.

atoms.name: discretisation of a continuous problem
atoms.essential_semantics: Replacing a continuous object by a finite one, with the discretisation parameter and the induced error explicit, and the continuous problem still represented.
atoms.canonical_example: replacing d/dx by a finite difference with step h
atoms.rationale: Discretisation is the paradigmatic lossy translation; whether the loss is recorded is the discriminating question.

atoms.name: error bound as a quantified statement
atoms.essential_semantics: A bound is a universally quantified claim over an input class, with the class and the norm stated, not a single observed discrepancy.
atoms.canonical_example: for all x in [0,1], |p(x) - f(x)| <= 1e-4
atoms.rationale: An error bound is a theorem about a method; reducing it to an empirical number removes its guarantee.

atoms.name: separation of exact and numeric evaluation paths
atoms.essential_semantics: The system distinguishes symbolic/exact evaluation from numeric evaluation and does not silently substitute one for the other.
atoms.canonical_example: sqrt(2) stays exact unless numeric evaluation is requested
atoms.rationale: Premature numeric evaluation destroys the ability to reason symbolically and silently introduces error.

atoms.name: finite-difference approximation of derivatives
atoms.essential_semantics: Difference quotient with a step size, carrying both truncation and rounding error, explicitly approximate.
atoms.canonical_example: (f(x+h) - f(x))/h approximates f'(x) with error O(h)
atoms.rationale: It is the canonical case where two error sources trade off, requiring the approximation to be explicit.

atoms.name: fixed-point iteration and contraction conditions
atoms.essential_semantics: Iterating a map with convergence guaranteed only under a contraction or similar condition.
atoms.canonical_example: x_{k+1} = g(x_k) converges if g is a contraction
atoms.rationale: The condition is what separates a convergent scheme from a divergent one and must be attachable.

atoms.name: floating-point number as a distinct type from the real
atoms.essential_semantics: A finite-precision representation with a declared format, which is not the mathematical real it approximates and for which arithmetic is not associative.
atoms.canonical_example: (a + b) + c differs from a + (b + c) in binary64
atoms.rationale: Identifying float with real is the foundational conflation of scientific computing and invalidates symbolic rewrites that assume exact arithmetic.

atoms.name: interpolation and its validity region
atoms.essential_semantics: Constructing a function through data with the interpolation scheme and the region of validity recorded; extrapolation is a distinct claim.
atoms.canonical_example: cubic spline through knots, invalid outside the knot range
atoms.rationale: Silent extrapolation beyond the data range is a routine and consequential misuse.

atoms.name: interval and validated arithmetic
atoms.essential_semantics: Computing with enclosures that provably contain the true value, at the cost of width growth.
atoms.canonical_example: [1.99, 2.01] contains the true value
atoms.rationale: It is the constructive counterpart to error bounds and shows that rigour is achievable numerically.

atoms.name: iterative method with a stated stopping rule
atoms.essential_semantics: An update rule, an initial value and a termination criterion, where the returned object is an approximation with a status.
atoms.canonical_example: iterate until ||x_{k+1} - x_k|| < tol or k > kmax
atoms.rationale: Whether the iteration converged is part of the result; returning only the final iterate hides failure.

atoms.name: numerical solution of linear systems
atoms.essential_semantics: Solving Ax = b as a computation with conditioning-dependent accuracy, distinct from forming A^{-1}.
atoms.canonical_example: solve(A, b) rather than inv(A) @ b
atoms.rationale: The mathematical statement and its numerical realisation differ; keeping both views is the point of a mathematical IR with backends.

atoms.name: machine epsilon and representable range
atoms.essential_semantics: The relative spacing of representable numbers, and the finite range with overflow and underflow thresholds.
atoms.canonical_example: eps for binary64 is about 2.2e-16
atoms.rationale: Every relative error bound is expressed in units of epsilon.

atoms.name: grid or mesh over a domain
atoms.essential_semantics: A finite set of points or cells covering a domain, with resolution and boundary handling as parameters.
atoms.canonical_example: a uniform grid with spacing h on [0, L]
atoms.rationale: Mesh resolution is a stated approximation parameter with a direct effect on error.

atoms.name: Monte Carlo estimation
atoms.essential_semantics: Estimating an expectation by sampling, with sample size, the resulting stochastic error, and the estimator's randomness explicit.
atoms.canonical_example: Ehat = (1/N) sum f(X_i) with standard error sigma/sqrt(N)
atoms.rationale: A Monte Carlo estimate is a random variable, not a number; representing it as a number hides its variability.

atoms.name: overflow, underflow and special values
atoms.essential_semantics: Infinities, NaN and subnormals as representable outcomes with defined propagation, distinguished from mathematical infinity and from undefinedness.
atoms.canonical_example: 0.0/0.0 yields NaN, which is not the mathematical statement 'undefined'
