atoms.rationale: Silent NaN propagation converts a definedness failure into a numeric value, hiding the mathematical error.

atoms.name: declared precision and number format
atoms.essential_semantics: The width and format (binary32/64, fixed point, arbitrary precision) is part of the numeric type and affects reproducibility.
atoms.canonical_example: computation in binary32 versus binary64
atoms.rationale: Precision is a semantic property of a computed result, not an implementation detail, once error bounds are claimed.

atoms.name: numerical integration
atoms.essential_semantics: Approximation of an integral with a rule, node count and an error estimate, and with the exact integral still representable.
atoms.canonical_example: Gauss-Legendre with n nodes approximates the integral
atoms.rationale: Replacing an integral by a quadrature sum without recording the substitution is silent semantic loss.

atoms.name: relative error
atoms.essential_semantics: Error normalised by the magnitude of the true value, dimensionless and undefined when the true value is zero.
atoms.rationale: The zero-denominator case is a genuine partiality that a tolerance-based comparison must handle explicitly.

atoms.name: reproducibility conditions of a computed result
atoms.essential_semantics: The set of conditions (precision, seed, ordering, library version) under which a numeric result is reproducible, recorded with the result.
atoms.canonical_example: parallel reduction order changes the last bits of a sum
atoms.rationale: A numeric claim without reproducibility conditions cannot be verified by anyone else.

atoms.name: pseudo-random generation and seeding
atoms.essential_semantics: Randomness is produced by a named generator with a seed; a pseudo-random draw is not a mathematical random variable.
atoms.canonical_example: results reproducible given generator and seed
atoms.rationale: The mathematical model of randomness and its computational simulation are different objects and both should be nameable.

atoms.name: numerical root finding
atoms.essential_semantics: Approximating solutions of f(x) = 0 with bracketing or initial guesses, returning an approximate root with an error indication.
atoms.canonical_example: bisection on [a,b] with f(a)f(b) < 0
atoms.rationale: A numerical root is not the exact solution set; the difference must be visible.

atoms.name: rounding mode and tie-breaking
atoms.essential_semantics: The rounding rule applied is stated (round-to-nearest-even, toward zero) since it changes results and error bounds.
atoms.canonical_example: round half to even makes 0.5 round to 0
atoms.rationale: Needed for bit-level reproducibility claims and for correct interval arithmetic.

atoms.name: sparsity and structural zeros
atoms.essential_semantics: A structural zero (known to be zero by the model) is distinct from a numerically small value, and sparsity patterns are part of the object.
atoms.canonical_example: a banded matrix whose off-band entries are structurally zero
atoms.rationale: The structural/numerical zero distinction affects both algorithms and model interpretation.

atoms.name: numerical stability of an algorithm
atoms.essential_semantics: A property of a method (backward or forward stability) as distinct from the conditioning of the problem it solves.
atoms.canonical_example: Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting is backward stable in practice
atoms.rationale: The problem/algorithm split is the core conceptual structure of numerical analysis and is easily conflated.

atoms.name: time integration scheme and stability condition
atoms.essential_semantics: Explicit or implicit schemes with step size and stability restrictions (e.g. CFL) attached.
atoms.canonical_example: forward Euler with dt below the stability limit
atoms.rationale: The stability condition is a constraint on the numerical method that has no analogue in the continuous statement and must be surfaced.

atoms.name: tolerance as an explicit parameter
atoms.essential_semantics: Convergence and equality tests carry an explicit tolerance and its type (absolute, relative, or combined); no hidden default is applied silently.
atoms.canonical_example: stop when the relative change is below 1e-8
atoms.rationale: A hidden tolerance turns a mathematical equality into an undocumented approximate one.

atoms.name: explicit ambiguity or underspecification
atoms.essential_semantics: The representation can mark that a statement is ambiguous or underspecified rather than silently choosing a reading.
atoms.canonical_example: 'average' is ambiguous between mean and median
atoms.rationale: Silently resolving an ambiguity manufactures content that was not present in the source; flagging it is the honest alternative.

atoms.name: explicit approximation claim with its basis
atoms.essential_semantics: A relation asserted only approximately, recording the approximation kind (asymptotic, numerical, first-order, modelling) and its validity regime.
atoms.canonical_example: the sampling distribution is approximately normal for large n
atoms.rationale: Almost every applied result is approximate in a specific, statable sense; erasing the sense is the largest single source of overclaiming.

atoms.name: speech-act distinction among statements
atoms.essential_semantics: Definitions, assumptions, assertions requiring justification, questions and goals are distinct kinds of statement, each with different obligations.
atoms.canonical_example: 'let x := 3' versus 'x = 3 must be shown'
atoms.rationale: Without this typing a system cannot tell what it must prove, what it may assume and what it has merely named.

atoms.name: explicit assumption
atoms.essential_semantics: A proposition taken as given for the purposes of a derivation, marked as assumed rather than established, and enumerable.
atoms.canonical_example: assume the errors are independent
atoms.rationale: The set of assumptions is what makes a result criticisable; a representation that cannot list its assumptions cannot support review.

atoms.name: causal claim with its identifying assumptions
atoms.essential_semantics: A causal statement carries the assumptions (no unmeasured confounding, positivity, consistency) under which it is identified.
atoms.canonical_example: the ATE is identified given the measured confounders
atoms.rationale: A causal effect estimate without its identifying assumptions is not interpretable and is routinely presented as if it were.

atoms.name: qualified belief attached to a statement
atoms.essential_semantics: A statement may carry an explicit degree of belief or a confidence level, with its interpretation stated, and the qualifier is not silently dropped.
atoms.canonical_example: with 95 percent confidence, the effect lies in [0.1, 0.4]
atoms.rationale: Dropping the qualifier converts a hedged claim into an unhedged one, the most common form of semantic inflation.

atoms.name: systematic consistency and well-formedness checking
atoms.essential_semantics: A mechanical check that a body of statements is type-correct, dimensionally consistent, scope-correct and free of unresolved names, with actionable rejection.
atoms.canonical_example: reject a model that uses an undeclared symbol
atoms.rationale: Rejection of ill-formed input is the primary product of a checked mathematical representation; a permissive checker adds no epistemic value.

atoms.name: detection of inconsistent assumptions or constraints
atoms.essential_semantics: The system can identify that a set of stated facts cannot all hold, and report which ones conflict.
atoms.canonical_example: x > 5 together with x < 3 is unsatisfiable
atoms.rationale: Silent inconsistency yields arbitrary conclusions; detection is a core value of a checked representation.

atoms.name: association, implication and causation kept distinct
atoms.essential_semantics: Statistical association, logical implication and causal influence are three different relations that must not share a representation.
atoms.canonical_example: X and Y are correlated does not license X causes Y or X implies Y
atoms.rationale: Collapsing these three is the single most consequential category error in quantitative reasoning, and it is a representational choice whether the collapse is possible.

atoms.name: counterexample as a refuting object
atoms.essential_semantics: A concrete instance refuting a universal claim, representable and checkable against the claim.
atoms.canonical_example: n = 4 refutes 'every natural number is prime'
atoms.rationale: Refutation is as much a part of reasoning as proof and requires instantiation machinery.

atoms.name: defeasible / non-monotonic inference
atoms.essential_semantics: Conclusions that can be withdrawn when further information arrives, marked as such and distinguished from deductive consequences.
atoms.canonical_example: by default assume stationarity, retract if a trend is detected
atoms.rationale: Applied reasoning is largely defeasible; presenting a defeasible conclusion as a deduction misstates its status.

atoms.name: evidential support distinguished from truth
atoms.essential_semantics: A statement may be supported to a degree by data without being asserted as true, and the support measure is named.
atoms.canonical_example: the data provide a Bayes factor of 12 in favour of H1
atoms.rationale: Evidence and truth are different; the distinction is what prevents statistical results from being reported as facts.

atoms.name: provenance of a value: given, derived or estimated
atoms.essential_semantics: Every quantity is marked as supplied data, derived by computation, or estimated from data, and derivation dependencies are recoverable.
atoms.canonical_example: sigmahat is estimated; sigma is a parameter; n is given
atoms.rationale: Confusing an estimate with a known constant is a standard route to overconfident conclusions.

atoms.name: idealising assumption marked as false-but-useful
atoms.essential_semantics: Assumptions known not to hold exactly (frictionless, infinite population, perfectly measured) are marked as idealisations rather than as facts.
atoms.canonical_example: assume the sample is drawn from an infinite population
atoms.rationale: Idealisations behave differently from believed assumptions when a model fails, and the distinction guides diagnosis.

atoms.name: explicitly unknown quantities
atoms.essential_semantics: A quantity may be declared unknown or not yet determined, distinct from being absent, zero, or defaulted.
atoms.canonical_example: sigma is unknown and must be estimated
atoms.rationale: Substituting a default for an unknown is a silent fabrication; representing unknown-ness prevents it.

atoms.name: locally scoped assumption
atoms.essential_semantics: An assumption in force only within a block, function body or branch, which does not leak to sibling or enclosing scopes and is discharged on exit.
atoms.canonical_example: inside the case x > 0, assume x > 0 and derive log(x) is defined
atoms.rationale: Case analysis and local reasoning depend on scoped hypotheses; a global assumption store makes case-splitting unsound.

atoms.name: model-world distinction
atoms.essential_semantics: Statements internal to a model are distinguished from claims about the world the model represents.
atoms.canonical_example: under the model, the residuals are normal; the data are not claimed to be
atoms.rationale: Model-internal truth reported as external fact is the characteristic failure of applied modelling.

atoms.name: descriptive statement versus decision rule
atoms.essential_semantics: A statement of how things are is distinguished from a rule about what should be done given them.
atoms.canonical_example: the posterior probability is 0.03 versus therefore reject the batch
atoms.rationale: Decision rules embed a loss function; keeping them separate from inference exposes that loss function to scrutiny.

atoms.name: conjecture and open question
atoms.essential_semantics: A well-formed statement whose truth value is not established, expressible without being asserted.
atoms.canonical_example: is P equal to NP?
atoms.rationale: The ability to state without asserting is a basic requirement for representing mathematical discourse.

atoms.name: epistemic status of a statement
atoms.essential_semantics: Proven, assumed, conjectured, refuted, unknown, or checked-by-computation as an explicit attribute of a statement.
atoms.canonical_example: the Riemann hypothesis has status conjectured
atoms.rationale: Mixing conjectures with theorems in the same representation without a status field makes downstream use unsafe.

atoms.name: provenance and attribution
atoms.essential_semantics: Where a statement, dataset or constant came from, recorded with the object rather than in surrounding prose.
atoms.canonical_example: the constant is from CODATA 2018
atoms.rationale: Traceability is what makes a derived result auditable; prose citations are not machine-checkable.

atoms.name: population or unit to which a claim applies
atoms.essential_semantics: The reference class of a claim (which population, which units, which time period) is part of the claim.
atoms.canonical_example: the effect estimate applies to adults aged 18 to 65 in the study population
atoms.rationale: Generalising beyond the sampled population is an inferential error that only an explicit reference class can flag.

atoms.name: sensitivity of a conclusion to its assumptions
atoms.essential_semantics: How much a conclusion changes when an assumption is varied, expressible as a derived statement linked to the assumption.
atoms.canonical_example: the conclusion reverses if the prior scale is doubled
atoms.rationale: Robustness of conclusions is itself a mathematical statement and depends on assumptions being addressable objects.

atoms.name: declared loss when moving between representations
atoms.essential_semantics: When a statement is translated into a weaker formalism, the specific facts dropped, approximated or weakened are enumerated and attached to the output.
atoms.canonical_example: translating a constrained model to an unconstrained solver drops the constraint sigma > 0, which must be reported
atoms.rationale: Interoperability literature (OpenMath phrasebooks, MathML content-to-presentation) treats lossy mapping as the normal case; silent loss produces authoritative-looking wrong output, the worst failure mode for a translating system.

atoms.name: domain of validity attached to a statement
atoms.essential_semantics: A result holds under stated conditions (range of inputs, regime, population), and using it outside them is detectable.
atoms.canonical_example: the linear approximation is valid for small displacements
atoms.rationale: Most misuse of correct results is out-of-domain application; carrying the domain makes it checkable.

atoms.name: safe renaming of bound variables
atoms.essential_semantics: Renaming binders to avoid capture without changing meaning, applied automatically where needed.
atoms.canonical_example: rename the inner bound i before substituting
atoms.rationale: Without it, substitution under binders is unsound; with it, structural equality becomes meaningful.

atoms.name: application reduction
atoms.essential_semantics: Substituting an argument into a function body, capture-avoiding, with evaluation order made explicit where it matters.
atoms.canonical_example: (x |-> x^2)(3) reduces to 9
atoms.rationale: It is the computational core of any language with function abstraction.

atoms.name: canonical form preserving semantics
atoms.essential_semantics: A deterministic map from semantically equal objects to one representation, which must not reorder non-commutative operands or drop information.
atoms.canonical_example: two alpha-equivalent statements canonicalise identically; A*B does not canonicalise to B*A
atoms.rationale: Canonicalisation is where semantics is most easily lost: an over-eager canonicaliser silently identifies distinct objects, which is worse than no canonicalisation.

atoms.name: proof or definition by exhaustive cases
atoms.essential_semantics: Splitting on a disjunction with exhaustiveness required and each branch carrying its case hypothesis.
atoms.canonical_example: consider x >= 0 and x < 0 separately
atoms.rationale: Non-exhaustive case analysis produces a gap in the argument that a representation can detect mechanically.

atoms.name: multiple faithful views of one object
atoms.essential_semantics: One semantic object may have several presentations (matrix and linear map, density and CDF, H- and V-representation) that are inter-derivable and marked as views, not as different objects.
atoms.canonical_example: a distribution presented by its pdf, its cdf and its characteristic function
atoms.rationale: Collapsing views loses information and privileging one view arbitrarily is a modelling decision that should be visible.

atoms.name: translation to an external system
atoms.essential_semantics: Mapping a statement into a target formalism or solver, where constructs unsupported by the target are reported rather than dropped.
atoms.canonical_example: compiling a constrained model to a solver that lacks the constraint type
atoms.rationale: Every practical mathematical IR is a translator; the honesty of that translation is its core quality attribute.

atoms.name: conditioning as a model transformation
atoms.essential_semantics: Transforming a joint model into a conditional one given observations, with the conditioning set explicit and normalisation acknowledged.
atoms.canonical_example: condition the generative model on the observed y
atoms.rationale: Inference is conditioning; representing it as an operation on models rather than a formula is what allows the same model to be queried many ways.

atoms.name: propagation of constraints and refinements
atoms.essential_semantics: Deriving consequences of declared constraints (positivity, bounds, shapes) and using them to discharge or generate obligations.
atoms.canonical_example: from sigma > 0 conclude log(sigma) is defined
atoms.rationale: Refinement types are useful only if their information is propagated; otherwise obligations are neither discharged nor reported.

atoms.name: reductio and contraposition
atoms.essential_semantics: Deriving falsity from an assumed negation, with the classical step marked where relevant.
atoms.canonical_example: assume sqrt(2) is rational and derive a contradiction
atoms.rationale: The assumption must be scoped and discharged; leaking it invalidates everything after the proof.

atoms.name: semantic difference between two versions of a statement
atoms.essential_semantics: Comparing two formulations and reporting the semantic delta (an assumption added, a bound weakened) rather than a textual diff.
atoms.canonical_example: version 2 weakens 'for all x' to 'for almost all x'
atoms.rationale: Model revision is a normal activity; a semantic diff is only possible if statements are structured objects.

atoms.name: chained equational derivation
atoms.essential_semantics: A sequence of steps each justified by an equality or inequality, with the relation composed correctly (equalities compose; approximations accumulate error).
atoms.canonical_example: a = b <= c gives a <= c
atoms.rationale: Chaining mixed relations requires knowing how they compose; treating approximate steps as exact silently loses the error budget.

atoms.name: partial evaluation with unknowns remaining
atoms.essential_semantics: Evaluating what can be evaluated while leaving symbolic unknowns in place, rather than failing or demanding all values.
atoms.canonical_example: 2 * x + 3 * 4 evaluates to 2 * x + 12
atoms.rationale: Mathematics is normally done with some quantities unknown; a representation that requires full valuation cannot do algebra.

atoms.name: introducing and using a witness
atoms.essential_semantics: Establishing an existential by exhibiting a witness, and using one by naming a fresh constant whose freshness is enforced.
atoms.canonical_example: let c be such that f(c) = 0, where c is fresh
atoms.rationale: Reusing a non-fresh name when eliminating an existential is unsound and is a classic proof-system bug.

atoms.name: applying induction
atoms.essential_semantics: Discharging a universal over an inductive domain by base and step, with the induction hypothesis available only in the step.
atoms.canonical_example: prove sum_{i<=n} i = n(n+1)/2 by induction on n
atoms.rationale: Using the induction hypothesis outside the step case is a classic unsound move that scoping prevents.

atoms.name: structured annotation of what a transformation lost
atoms.essential_semantics: A machine-readable record distinguishing dropped, approximated and weakened content, attached to the transformation output.
atoms.canonical_example: the unit annotation was dropped; the equality was weakened to approximate equality
atoms.rationale: Prose warnings are not checkable; a typed loss record is what makes downstream consumers able to react to the loss.

atoms.name: marginalisation as an inference operation
atoms.essential_semantics: Eliminating variables from a joint model by summation or integration, with the eliminated variable recorded and the operation type-correct.
atoms.canonical_example: marginalise the latent class out of the joint likelihood
atoms.rationale: It is the fundamental probabilistic-inference transformation and a binder-eliminating operation with real preconditions.

atoms.name: detachment from an implication
atoms.essential_semantics: From P and P implies Q infer Q, with the hypothesis discharged and recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: from continuity and the hypotheses of the MVT, conclude the existence of c
atoms.rationale: Applying a theorem requires checking its hypotheses; a system that applies results without checking them produces unjustified conclusions.

atoms.name: derivation of moments from a distribution
atoms.essential_semantics: Computing expectations of functions of a random variable from the distribution object, symbolically where possible, with existence conditions checked.
atoms.canonical_example: E[X^2] for X ~ Normal(mu, sigma^2) equals mu^2 + sigma^2
atoms.rationale: It tests whether a distribution is a semantic object that can be reasoned about or merely a sampler.

atoms.name: normal form of an expression
atoms.essential_semantics: A distinguished representative reached by exhaustive rewriting, with confluence and termination as stated properties.
atoms.canonical_example: conjunctive normal form of a propositional formula
atoms.rationale: Normal forms are only well-defined if the rewrite system is confluent; asserting a normal form without confluence is unjustified.

atoms.name: structural pattern matching on expressions
atoms.essential_semantics: Matching an expression against a pattern with metavariables, respecting binders and types.
atoms.canonical_example: match a + b * c against the pattern ?x + ?y
atoms.rationale: All rule-based transformation begins with matching; ignoring binders makes matching unsound.

atoms.name: quantifier movement and prenex form
atoms.essential_semantics: Moving quantifiers outward with the correct dual switching under negation and correct handling of free variables.
atoms.canonical_example: not (forall x P) becomes exists x not P
atoms.rationale: Quantifier movement is where order errors are introduced; the transformation must preserve alternation.

atoms.name: independent checking of a derivation
atoms.essential_semantics: A derivation can be validated by a checker that does not trust the producer, ideally with a small trusted core.
atoms.canonical_example: a kernel re-checks every inference step
atoms.rationale: It is the defining capability of a formal mathematical system and the top of the maturity ladder.

atoms.name: quantifier elimination in decidable theories
atoms.essential_semantics: Producing an equivalent quantifier-free formula in theories that admit it, with the theory identified.
atoms.canonical_example: eliminating x from exists x. ax^2 + bx + c = 0 over the reals
atoms.rationale: It is the boundary between statable and decidable; noting where it applies is useful for a reasoning IR.

atoms.name: querying a body of mathematical statements
atoms.essential_semantics: The representation supports asking structural questions (which statements assume independence, which involve this variable, which are approximate) mechanically.
atoms.canonical_example: list every statement whose validity depends on normality
atoms.rationale: A representation earns its cost by being queryable; otherwise prose plus code is sufficient.

atoms.name: directed rewriting with rules
atoms.essential_semantics: Oriented equations applied to transform expressions, with termination and side conditions attached to each rule.
atoms.canonical_example: rewrite x + 0 to x
atoms.rationale: Rewriting without side conditions is exactly how symbolic systems produce domain-narrowing errors.

atoms.name: round-trip fidelity between surface and internal form
atoms.essential_semantics: Parsing then printing (and re-parsing) yields a semantically identical object, with any normalisation documented.
atoms.canonical_example: parse, print, re-parse and compare canonical forms
atoms.rationale: Round-trip failure is the cheapest mechanical evidence that a representation is losing information.

atoms.name: verification that a transformation preserves meaning
atoms.essential_semantics: A transformation is accompanied by a check or proof that its output denotes the same object, or by an explicit declaration of what changed.
atoms.canonical_example: verify that a rewritten objective has the same minimisers
atoms.rationale: Unverified transformations are the mechanism by which correct inputs become incorrect outputs without any error being raised.

atoms.name: simplification with preserved meaning
atoms.essential_semantics: Reducing expression complexity while preserving denotation, including the domain of definition and any attached qualifiers.
atoms.canonical_example: simplifying sqrt(x^2) to |x|, not to x
atoms.rationale: Simplification that changes the domain is the single most common symbolic-system bug and is entirely a semantics question.

atoms.name: Skolemisation of existentials
atoms.essential_semantics: Replacing an existential under universals by a function of those universals, preserving satisfiability but not equivalence, with the transformation recorded.
atoms.canonical_example: forall x exists y P(x,y) becomes forall x P(x, f(x))
atoms.rationale: It is a semantics-changing transformation that is legitimate only for satisfiability; performing it silently misrepresents the statement.

atoms.name: solving a relation for an unknown
atoms.essential_semantics: Producing the solution set with the domain conditions and branch choices recorded, not a single root.
atoms.canonical_example: solving x^2 = 4 gives {2, -2}
atoms.rationale: Dropping a branch of a solution is a silent loss that changes the mathematics.

atoms.name: explicit staging of symbolic and numeric phases
atoms.essential_semantics: When symbolic manipulation ends and numeric evaluation begins is explicit and controllable, not implicit.
atoms.canonical_example: differentiate symbolically, then evaluate numerically at x = 2
atoms.rationale: Premature numericisation is irreversible; making the boundary explicit preserves the ability to reason.

atoms.name: substitution of equals for equals
atoms.essential_semantics: Replacing a subterm by an equal one, valid only in extensional contexts and not under binders that capture.
atoms.canonical_example: from a = b infer f(a) = f(b)
atoms.rationale: Congruence of equality is the most-used inference step and has real side conditions in intensional or approximate contexts.

atoms.name: symbolic differentiation
atoms.essential_semantics: Producing a derivative expression with respect to a named variable, including correct handling of piecewise and non-differentiable points.
atoms.canonical_example: d/dx of x sin(x) is sin(x) + x cos(x)
atoms.rationale: Differentiating a piecewise function at a break point without a caveat produces a value where none exists.

atoms.name: symbolic integration with failure as an outcome
atoms.essential_semantics: Attempting a closed form and reporting failure explicitly rather than returning an unevaluated or wrong result silently.
atoms.canonical_example: integral of exp(-x^2) has no elementary antiderivative
atoms.rationale: Honest failure is a required behaviour; silently substituting a numeric method changes the claim.

atoms.name: dependency ordering and cycle detection
atoms.essential_semantics: Definitions and model statements are ordered by dependency, with cycles detected and reported rather than silently resolved.
atoms.canonical_example: detect that a and b are defined in terms of each other
atoms.rationale: Generative models and definition blocks must be acyclic; unchecked cycles produce non-terminating or meaningless evaluation.

atoms.name: inference and checking of types
atoms.essential_semantics: Deriving types for unannotated terms and rejecting ill-typed ones with a localised, informative error.
atoms.canonical_example: infer that mu + sigma * z is Real given the components
atoms.rationale: Type inference is the mechanism by which a representation actually enforces its distinctions; without it, declared types are decoration.

atoms.name: unification of terms and types
atoms.essential_semantics: Solving for a substitution making two terms equal, with occurs-check and type compatibility.
atoms.canonical_example: unify f(?x, b) with f(a, ?y) giving ?x = a, ?y = b
atoms.rationale: It is the engine of type inference and of rule application; without occurs-check it produces circular nonsense.

atoms.name: instantiating a universal statement
atoms.essential_semantics: Replacing a universally bound variable by a term of the right type from the stated domain.
atoms.canonical_example: from 'for all real x, x^2 >= 0' conclude '(-3)^2 >= 0'
atoms.rationale: Instantiating with a term outside the quantification domain is a common and detectable error.
